cna.title: Action Pack: Possible IP spoofing in Action Dispatch RemoteIp

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. From 8.1 until 8.1.4.1, Since Rails 8.1.0, ActionDispatch::RemoteIp derives request.remote_ip from Rack::Request#forwarded_for, which under Rack 3 reads the RFC 7239 Forwarded header in preference to X-Forwarded-For. When a reverse proxy appends the client address to X-Forwarded-For but passes a client-supplied Forwarded header through unchanged, request.remote_ip returns an address chosen by the client, and the IP spoofing check does not raise, because it compares only Client-Ip with the forwarded addresses. An unauthenticated attacker could therefore spoof request.remote_ip, possibly bypassing IP-based access controls and rate limits keyed on the client address (including the default by: of rate_limit), and falsifying the client address in logs. An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements: Runs Rails 8.1.0 through 8.1.4 with Rack 3. Under Rack 2.2, forwarded_for reads only X-Forwarded-For. Is served behind a proxy that does not remove or overwrite a client-supplied Forwarded header. Relies on request.remote_ip for access control, rate limiting, or auditing. The fix detects a spoofed Forwarded header only when the proxy also sets X-Forwarded-For. An application whose proxy passes a client-supplied Forwarded header through and sets no X-Forwarded-For remains exposed after upgrading, and should configure the proxy to remove or overwrite Forwarded, or apply the workaround below. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.4.1.

descriptions.description: CWE-348: Use of Less Trusted Source

cna.title: SPARQL Injection in MISP Wikidata Lookup Module via Unescaped User Input

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: Improve Wikidata enrichment and return MISP standard

x_patch2vuln.subject: Improve Wikidata enrichment and return MISP standard
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The vulnerability is remediated by properly escaping user-supplied text as a SPARQL string literal using json.dumps with ensure_ascii=False, which neutralizes quotes, backslashes, newlines, and control characters. Additional hardening includes strict validation of the language tag, numeric configuration values, text length, and UUID format before query construction; validation of Wikidata response structure and entity URI format before importing results; replacement of raw exception formatting with generic error messages that do not expose upstream details; use of the modern Wikidata SPARQL endpoint with POST method; a proper MISP user-agent string; and a bounded request timeout.
assumptions: The CAPEC-143 mapping is the closest available pattern; no SPARQL-specific CAPEC exists in the catalog. The underlying technique (query injection via unsanitized string concatenation) is identical to SQL injection.

CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker has authenticated access to a MISP instance with the wiki expansion module enabled. The actual privilege level required depends on MISP role configuration, which is not specified in the patch.

The affected version range is unspecified; the patch does not include version tags or release boundaries. The vulnerability existed in module version 0.2 (as indicated by the old moduleinfo) and was fixed in version 1.0.
The CVSS VI:L rating accounts for both the query manipulation and the old error-message information disclosure. If only the injection is considered (without the error leak), VI could be rated N.

The patch is treated as a single vulnerability fix (SPARQL injection) with associated hardening changes (error sanitization, input validation, endpoint update). The caller asserts all changes relate to the same vulnerability.
No evidence of active exploitation, PoC, or in-the-wild usage was found in the patch or metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: The patch rewrites the wiki.py handler to: (1) escape user text via json.dumps(text, ensure_ascii=False) before embedding in the SPARQL query; (2) validate language tags with a regex, numeric settings (max_results 1-25, timeout 1-60), text length (1-2000 chars), and UUID format; (3) switch from string concatenation to a properly escaped SPARQL literal; (4) use the modern https://query.wikidata.org/sparql endpoint with POST method and a MISP user-agent; (5) validate Wikidata response bindings and entity URIs against a strict pattern before creating annotation objects; (6) replace the mutable shared misperrors dict and raw exception formatting with a ModuleError class and generic error strings; (7) add a 313-line test suite (tests/test_wiki.py) covering injection vectors, invalid inputs, malformed responses, and error sanitization; (8) update documentation and module metadata to reflect the new misp_standard output format and configuration options.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The module is invoked over the network via the MISP API. AC:L: The injection requires only crafting a text value with SPARQL metacharacters; no race conditions or complex prerequisites. AT:N: No need to manipulate the attack target. PR:L: Requires authenticated access to a MISP instance with the wiki module enabled. UI:N: No user interaction beyond the API call. VC:N: The queried data is public Wikidata; no confidential MISP data is exposed. VI:L: An attacker can alter the enrichment results (integrity of advisory annotations) and the old error path could leak internal details. VA:N: No meaningful availability impact on the MISP system. SC/SI/SA:N: No impact on external systems beyond the public Wikidata service. Overall severity is low given the limited blast radius.

capecRationale.rationale: CAPEC-143 describes injection of query language fragments through unsanitized input into a dynamically constructed query. Although the CAPEC name references SQL specifically, the attack pattern is identical: an attacker supplies input containing query-language metacharacters (quotes, braces, keywords) that alter the structure of the query sent to an interpreter. SPARQL injection follows the same pattern. This is the closest available CAPEC; no SPARQL-specific CAPEC exists in the catalog. The uncertainty is that the CAPEC is SQL-specific in naming, but the underlying technique (query injection via string concatenation) is the same.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The module dynamically constructs a SPARQL query by concatenating untrusted user input directly into the query string without neutralizing special elements. This is the same pattern as code/query injection: the intended query structure is modified by attacker-controlled input. SPARQL is a query language interpreted by the Wikidata endpoint, making this a code injection into a query interpreter.

The old code formatted raw exception objects into the error response string ('wikidata API not accessible {}'.format(e)), which could expose internal details such as proxy credentials, full query text, or upstream response bodies. The fix replaces this with generic error messages.

solutions.value: The vulnerability is remediated by properly escaping user-supplied text as a SPARQL string literal using json.dumps with ensure_ascii=False, which neutralizes quotes, backslashes, newlines, and control characters. Additional hardening includes strict validation of the language tag, numeric configuration values, text length, and UUID format before query construction; validation of Wikidata response structure and entity URI format before importing results; replacement of raw exception formatting with generic error messages that do not expose upstream details; use of the modern Wikidata SPARQL endpoint with POST method; a proper MISP user-agent string; and a bounded request timeout.

descriptions.value: The Wikidata Lookup expansion module (wiki.py) in MISP misp-modules contained a SPARQL injection vulnerability. The handler function constructed a SPARQL query by directly concatenating the user-supplied text value into the query string without any escaping or parameterization: 'SELECT ?item WHERE { ?item rdfs:label"' + request.get("text") + '" @en }'. An authenticated MISP user with access to the module could supply a crafted text attribute value containing SPARQL syntax (quotes, closing braces, UNION, SERVICE, LIMIT, etc.) to alter the structure of the query sent to the Wikidata SPARQL endpoint. This could allow an attacker to modify the query logic, extract unintended data, or cause the query to fail in ways that expose internal error details. Additionally, the old error handling path formatted raw exception objects into the response string ('wikidata API not accessible {}'.format(e)), potentially leaking internal information such as proxy credentials, query contents, or response bodies. The module also used a spoofed browser user-agent string and the deprecated Wikidata endpoint. The vulnerability required authenticated access to the MISP instance and the ability to invoke the wiki expansion module with a text attribute. The impact is limited to manipulation of the enrichment query and potential disclosure of internal error details; it does not directly compromise the MISP server or its stored data.

cna.title: Action Pack: Possible cache poisoning in Action Pack content negotiation

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, Action Pack negotiates the format of a rendered response from the Accept, X-Requested-With and, for XHR requests without Accept, Content-Type request headers, but ActionController::Rendering#_set_vary_header adds Vary: Accept only when the request carries a usable Accept header and the response has no Vary header yet. A response to a request without Accept, or to an XHR request, therefore omits the headers that selected its representation, and a response whose Vary the application set before rendering (for example Vary: Accept-Language) never gains Accept. A shared cache that honours Vary could store such a response and serve it to later clients that request a different representation, possibly leading to cache poisoning in which visitors receive, until the entry expires, a page without its layout or HTML in place of JSON. The attacker cannot choose the content of the response. Applications that render negotiated responses from actions marked public (for example with expires_in ..., public: true) behind a shared cache that honours Vary, such as Thruster or Rack::Cache, are affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_live_view allows an authenticated user to mount a router-mounted LiveView without the on_mount hooks of its live_session via a phx_join message that carries neither a "url" nor a "redirect" key.

The catch-all clause of the private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex accepts a join without a URL for any session, including a root LiveView mounted at the router. The channel then mounts the LiveView with no route, and only a route adds the live_session hooks to the mount lifecycle. Checks that those hooks perform on the connected mount do not run, and event checks that they attach through attach_hook/4 are never attached. The attacker needs a valid session token for the LiveView, which only the HTTP render issues, after the hooks pass there. on_mount hooks declared in the LiveView module still run.

This issue affects phoenix_live_view: from 0.16.0 before 1.0.20, from 1.1.0-rc.0 before 1.1.34, and from 1.2.0-rc.0 before 1.2.14.

The target application has a live_session whose on_mount hook halts the mount for a suspended account and attaches a :handle_event hook with attach_hook/4 that denies the delete_post event to users who are not admins. The LiveView at /posts does not define handle_params/3.

  1. Sign in as a user without the admin role and load /posts over HTTP. Keep the session cookie, the CSRF token from the page, and the id, data-phx-session, and data-phx-static attributes of the element that has data-phx-main.
  2. Open the LiveView websocket at /live/websocket with the session cookie and the CSRF token.
  3. Send a phx_join message on the topic lv:<id>. The payload has "params" (with "_csrf_token" and "_mounts": 0), "session", and "static". It has no "url" key and no "redirect" key.
  4. The server replies with status ok. The LiveView is mounted without the live_session hooks.
  5. Send an event message of type click for the event delete_post. The LiveView handles the event, and the post is deleted.

The same join with the "url" key set to the page URL runs the hooks, and the delete_post event is denied. If the account is suspended after step 1, the join with "url" is refused, and the join without "url" still succeeds.

supportingMedia.value:
1. Join authorization. The private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex has three clauses. The "redirect" clause resolves the route and checks that it stays in the same live_session. The "url" clause requires, for a session where Phoenix.LiveView.Session.main?/1 is true, that the route for the URL matches the view and the live_session of the session. The third clause matches any other join parameters and returns the session with no route and no URL. Nested LiveViews need this clause because they have no URL. The clause does not call Phoenix.LiveView.Session.main?/1, so it also accepts a root LiveView that was mounted at the router.

2. Mount with no route. With no route, mount/3 receives :not_mounted_at_router as its params. The private load_lifecycle/2 adds the on_mount hooks of the live_session only when it receives a %Phoenix.LiveView.Route{}. Without a route it returns the lifecycle of the LiveView module alone. The live_session layout is skipped in the same way.

3. Result. The signed session token, the static token, the CSRF token, and the session cookie are all valid, so the join succeeds. The LiveView runs without the live_session hooks. Hooks that halt the mount do not run, and hooks attached with attach_hook/4 for :handle_event or :handle_info are never attached.

Conditions that stop the mount. A LiveView that defines handle_params/3 raises on a mount without a route. A LiveView whose mount/3 matches its params as a map raises. A LiveView that reads an assign that a skipped hook sets raises. In these cases the join fails.

The official JavaScript client always sends "url" or "redirect" for a root LiveView. Only nested views join without either key.

cna.title: Action Pack: Possible Strong Parameters bypass in Parameters#each_key

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActionController::Parameters#each_key delegates to the internal ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess that holds the request parameters, so when called with a block it returns that hash instead of the Parameters instance. The hash does not respond to permitted?, so Active Model mass assignment (new, assign_attributes, update) accepts it without raising ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError. An application that passes the return value of each_key to mass assignment could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to set attributes that the application does not permit, such as an authorization flag. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2020-8164, which made each, each_pair and each_value return the Parameters instance but left each_key delegated. An application is affected if it passes the return value of ActionController::Parameters#each_key, called with a block, to mass assignment. Rails itself makes no such call. cna.title: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode

descriptions.value: Action Pack is a framework for handling and responding to web requests. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, When ActionDispatch::Cookies reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations) or in the format that a :hybrid cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores request.session_options[:skip]. ActiveStorage::DisableSession relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in Set-Cookie on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its Set-Cookie header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users. Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a :hybrid serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores Set-Cookie on public responses. This is a path around the fix for CVE-2024-26144. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8. Its web services listener reads, once for each connection and before the TLS handshake, the IP range that decides for the address, and closes the connection without an answer when that range allows none of SMTP, POP3 and IMAP - every auto-ban, and an administrator's range that allows nothing - or when the ranges cannot be read; an address no range holds is let in, and loopback and the addresses in WebServicesTrustedProxies are never refused by a range. A connection opened before the ban has at most one guess after it, since every failed sign-in closes its connection. After the upgrade an administrator's range that allows none of the three also closes this listener - MTA-STS, ACME http-01 when this listener answers it, CalDAV, CardDAV, Autodiscover, autoconfiguration, the Web Key Directory, security.txt, the S/MIME root and CRL and the Apple profiles - to the addresses it holds, and such a refusal by a range that does not expire is named in the application log, once an hour for each address. Until then, keep WebServicesHttpsPort at 0 or reachable from trusted networks only, or block the listener's ports below the server: an AutoBanCommand of the administrator's own, which is run for every ban the server writes, can block the address on the listener's ports as well as on the ports it is told, for as long as the ban lasts; on Linux, turning the packaged fail2ban jail on (it is off as packaged) and adding the listener's ports to its port line blocks there, by the jail's own count (five matching lines within ten minutes as packaged; maxretry = 3 and findtime = 30m match the auto-ban's defaults), an address that goes on failing at the listener, where application logging is on (off by default), since its filter matches the "Auto-ban: logon failure" lines these sign-ins write. Turning on the per-name lockout (AccountLockoutThreshold above 0) limits the guesses at each account wherever they come from, within its separate defect. A rate-limiting proxy in front of the listener limits the guessing, but its clients' failures then ban the proxy's own address at the mail listeners unless that address is in AutoBanNeverBan.

descriptions.value: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 does not apply the server's IP ranges to the connections it accepts, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords at the listener's sign-ins after the auto-ban has banned the attacker's address. The listener is off by default (WebServicesHttpPort and WebServicesHttpsPort 0). From 6.3.3 its CardDAV, and from 6.3.4 its CalDAV and its Outlook Autodiscover answer to a request that carries credentials, sign an account in with HTTP Basic over HTTPS. A failed sign-in there counts towards the auto-ban as a failed logon on any other protocol does: when the failures counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 within 30 minutes by default), the server writes an IP range that refuses the address for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default), and the SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listeners refuse it. The web services listener asked no IP range when it accepted a connection (in 6.3.3 nothing, from 6.3.4 the country policy alone), so it went on serving such an address, whether its ban had been earned there or on another protocol, and also an address that an administrator's IP range allowing nothing holds. Each failed sign-in there closed only its own connection, and the next connection was accepted, during the ban and after it. The firewall rule and command the auto-ban can drive (AutoBanFirewall and AutoBanCommand, off by default) are told only the SMTP, POP3 and IMAP ports, so that the firewall rule and the packaged hook did not close the listener's ports, and the fail2ban jail packaged for Linux (off by default) lists only the mail and ManageSieve ports. The only limit left on the guesses at one account there was the per-name lockout (AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default), which has a separate defect fixed in the same release. The flaw is reached on the listener's HTTPS port: behind a TLS-terminating proxy the listener sees the proxy's address for every client, and a ban never named the client there.

cna.title: Unverified Ownership in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose setup looks, before it stops the service and again once the folders are hardened, at everything in Bin and ControlPanel, on the program folder's own level, and in Addons, Events, DBScripts, WebAdmin, Languages and MySQL, and refuses with exit code 7 to install where a program, a library, a script, a settings file or a folder there is owned by anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators or TrustedInstaller, has an owner that cannot be read, or has an entry of its own that lets another account change it, naming each with the icacls that deals with it and a restart of Windows before setup runs again. Until then, install hMailServer under Program Files, or into a new folder inside one that only administrators may change. Before running setup into or over a program folder that other accounts could write, list the owners from an elevated Command Prompt - dir /q /a "<program folder>" and dir /q /s /a over its Bin, ControlPanel, Events, WebAdmin, DBScripts, Addons, Languages and MySQL, as the hMailServer documentation, ServiceAccount.md, "Before upgrading an installation at a drive's root", gives them for all but MySQL - and the entries of their own, with icacls "<program folder>" and icacls "<folder>" /T over the same folders, where an entry not marked (I) that gives anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators or TrustedInstaller a right to change the item is another account's (the service's own Modify on hMailServerApiKeys.ini in Bin apart); where anybody but those owns anything there, or has such an entry, do not install over it: reinstall into a new folder as that page's "Reinstalling into a new folder" says.

descriptions.value: Unverified ownership in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when setup installs into, or upgrades, a program folder that accounts other than the administrators could write before, such as one made beforehand at the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but setup refused nothing that was already in them, or in the folders that hold the event script, the add-ons and the database scripts: a program, a library, a script or a settings file that another account owns, or whose own permissions let another account change it, is kept with that owner and those permissions, which the hardening of the folders does not take away. Setup then runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, and the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, runs them and the event script, so that a library such an account placed in Bin is loaded in place of the system's; the account can still change the file after the installation. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

cna.title: basic-ftp: Uncaught TypeError in MLSD directory-listing parser via __proto__ fact name causes DoS in Client.list()

descriptions.value: basic-ftp is an FTP client for Node.js. Prior to 6.2.4, the MLSD directory-listing parser in src/parseListMLSD.ts uses untrusted fact names from the FTP server as keys in the plain-object factHandlersByName dictionary without checking that the resolved property is an own handler. A fact named __proto__ therefore resolves to Object.prototype, bypasses the missing-handler guard, and is called as though it were a function, producing a TypeError. The error propagates through Client.list() and APIs that depend on it because it is not an FTPError. A malicious or compromised FTP server, or an on-path attacker on a plaintext FTP session, can make the affected operation reject, and the Node.js process terminates under the default behavior in Node.js 15 and later only if the application leaves that rejection unhandled. This issue is fixed in version 6.2.4.

cna.title: Philips Hue Bridge HomeKit Accessory Protocol chacha20_decrypt Integer Underflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

source.value: Sang Nguyen Thien (@gnas0x0018) and mistsu of Team ANHTUD

descriptions.value:
Philips Hue Bridge HomeKit Accessory Protocol chacha20_decrypt Integer Underflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Philips Hue Bridge. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the HomeKit Accessory Protocol service, which listens on TCP port 8080 by default. When parsing pairing requests, the process does not properly validate user-supplied data, which can result in an integer underflow before writing to memory. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the device. Was ZDI-CAN-28332.

cna.title: vLLM 0.10.1 before 0.31.0 Cohere2 Vision DoS via max_patches

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: vLLM 0.10.1 before 0.31.0 Cohere2 Vision DoS via max_patches

descriptions.value: vLLM from 0.10.1 before 0.31.0 forwards a request-controlled mm_processor_kwargs.max_patches value to the Hugging Face processor for Cohere2 Vision models without a server-side upper bound, causing quadratic CPU work during multimodal preprocessing. Remote clients can send small image chat-completion requests with large, varying max_patches values to bypass the LRU cache, exhaust preprocessing workers, and deny service to other clients.

cna.title: AutomatorWP Pro Webhooks addon <= 1.4.4 - Missing Authorization to Unauthenticated Arbitrary User Password Reset / Account Takeover via Webhook with 'Is the user ID' Field

descriptions.value: The AutomatorWP Pro plugin for WordPress' webhook addon is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 1.4.4. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to reset the password of any WordPress account, including administrators, resulting in full account takeover. This is only exploitable when an administrator has configured an automation pairing a Receive Webhook trigger — with an 'Is the user ID' field — to an Update-User action whose User ID field is left blank and whose Password field is mapped to the webhook password tag, which is a documented, supported plugin configuration.

cna.title: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with certain exploded expressions

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.3.0 until 2.9.1, URI template expressions using the explode modifier with the slash, dot, semicolon, question-mark, or ampersand operators generate ambiguous regular expressions. When Template#match or Template#extract processes an attacker-controlled URI beginning with the operator's leading character, optional member separators allow catastrophic backtracking and denial of service on MRI Ruby before 3.2 and JRuby. Addressable 2.9.0 incompletely remediated the earlier template issue because its tests did not reach these operator-prefixed paths. URI parsing and Template#expand are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

cna.title: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server SQL injection through custom pl-do tool parameters

descriptions.value: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, custom pl-do tools interpolated JSON arguments into a PostgreSQL DO block delimited by fixed dollar-quote tags. An argument containing $mcp_custom_tool$ could terminate the block and inject arbitrary SQL statements, while $mcp_args$ could inject procedural code into a plpgsql block. Because the statement used the simple query protocol, injected text could include additional statements and transaction control, bypassing read_only and accessing data or modifying resources available to the connecting role. The issue requires at least one pl-do custom tool; sql and pl-func tools pass arguments as bind parameters and are not affected by this injection mechanism. This issue is fixed in 1.1.0.

descriptions.description: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

cna.title: Docker Sandboxes privilege escalation through untrusted state directories

scenarios.value: A local unprivileged attacker controls a state or configuration directory reused by a root invocation with an attacker-influenced HOME or XDG_STATE_HOME.

solutions.value: Upgrade Docker Sandboxes to version 0.53.0 or later.

workarounds.value: Avoid running sbx or sandboxd as root. If a privileged invocation is required, use HOME and XDG_STATE_HOME values belonging to the target account and ensure its state and configuration directories are not controlled by another user.

descriptions.value: Docker Sandboxes reuses existing state and configuration directories without verifying their ownership. If sbx or sandboxd is run as root with HOME or, on Linux, XDG_STATE_HOME pointing to an attacker-controlled location, a local unprivileged user can substitute control-plane sockets and configuration trusted by the root process, potentially executing commands as root. Exploitation requires a privileged invocation with an attacker-influenced environment. The issue affects Linux and macOS and is fixed in version 0.53.0.

cna.title: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server custom tools performed writes without user confirmation

descriptions.value: pgEdge Postgres MCP Server enables SQL queries against PostgreSQL databases through Model Context Protocol compatible clients. Prior to 1.1.0, the bundled clients, including the CLI and web client, decided whether to request write confirmation by checking only for the query_database tool name instead of server-published write annotations. Custom pl-do, pl-func, and writing sql tools therefore ran without confirmation on allow_writes connections, including when a model followed instructions in retrieved content. The affected control is a bundled-client warning rather than a server authorization boundary, and other MCP clients do not inherit that prompt. This issue is fixed in 1.1.0.

cna.title: @hono/node-server: WebSocket upgrade request-target starting with `//` replaces the host in `c.req.url`, bypassing `Origin` checks

descriptions.value: @hono/node-server allows running the Hono application on Node.js. From 2.0.0 until 2.1.6, the WebSocket upgrade path resolves a raw request-target beginning with // against a base URL built from the Host header, causing the WHATWG URL parser to treat the request-target as a network-path reference and replace the host in c.req.url. Routing still uses the local WebSocket path, so an application that compares the Origin header with the origin of c.req.url, including checks implemented with csrf(), compares an attacker's origin with itself and accepts the connection. A page on another site can consequently open a WebSocket with the victim's cookies and read and send messages when the application uses upgradeWebSocket and trusts the host in c.req.url. Ordinary HTTP requests are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.6.

descriptions.description: CWE-1385: Missing Origin Validation in WebSockets

cna.title: Node.js is vulnerable to a remotely triggerable uncaught exception in TLS servers via deferred handshake callbacks

descriptions.value: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to terminate the server process. When a TLS server uses any of the SNICallback, OCSPRequest, newSession, or resumeSession hooks, or server.addContext(), the corresponding OpenSSL callbacks are deferred, and the deferred code does not handle the underlying socket being destroyed between scheduling and execution. By sending a client hello that reaches the vulnerable path (for example, no SNI together with an OCSP request) followed by padding and a socket FIN, an attacker makes OpenSSL deliver the client hello and the end-of-file in the same tick, so the socket is destroyed before the deferred callback runs and the process raises an uncaught exception instead of emitting an 'error' event. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

supportingMedia.value: A deferred-callback use-after-destroy in Node.js TLS server handshake handling allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to terminate the server process. When a TLS server uses any of the `SNICallback`, `OCSPRequest`, `newSession`, or `resumeSession` hooks, or `server.addContext()`, the corresponding OpenSSL callbacks are deferred, and the deferred code does not handle the underlying socket being destroyed between scheduling and execution. By sending a client hello that reaches the vulnerable path (for example, no SNI together with an OCSP request) followed by padding and a socket FIN, an attacker makes OpenSSL deliver the client hello and the end-of-file in the same tick, so the socket is destroyed before the deferred callback runs and the process raises an uncaught exception instead of emitting an `'error'` event. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

cna.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in Action View highlight helper

descriptions.value: Action View is a framework for handling view template lookup and rendering and provides view helpers for building HTML. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight substitutes each matched phrase into the :highlighter string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the <a href="search?q=\1"> form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a :highlighter that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default <mark>\1</mark> highlighter and the block form are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Tornado: Open redirect via triple-slash redirect paths

descriptions.value: Tornado is a Python web framework and asynchronous networking library. In versions through 6.6.0, applications using  tornado.web.RedirectHandler  with URL templates that allow attacker-controlled substitutions to influence the destination can be vulnerable to an open redirect using three or more leading slashes. Differences between Python’s URL parsing and browser URL interpretation allow a crafted destination to redirect a user to an attacker-controlled host. The remediation for CVE-2026-116578 in version 6.6.0 did not fully address this case. This issue is fixed in version 6.6.1.

cna.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode can decode Punycode labels that contain bidirectional controls, zero-width characters, control characters, or other default-ignorable format characters. Addressable::URI#display_uri can consequently show a reordered or visually indistinguishable hostname even though host, normalized_host, and network connections use the original encoded hostname. The pure-Ruby backend accepts the full prohibited set, while the native libidn backend is affected from 2.5.2 for characters added after Unicode 3.2. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

cna.title: express-rate-limit skipFailedRequests / skipSuccessfulRequests: with the default MemoryStore, a request from an earlier window is still un-counted from the current window

descriptions.value: express-rate-limit is a basic rate-limiting middleware for Express. From 8.6.0 until 8.7.2, the built-in MemoryStore returns a Client whose mutable resetTime object is retained by middleware using skipFailedRequests or skipSuccessfulRequests. When a later request resets the client window, MemoryStore.resetClient mutates that same Date, so an earlier request that finishes or disconnects after the reset can pass the stale-window guard and decrement the current window's count. A client able to keep requests in flight across the boundary can obtain a bounded extra burst of up to one additional configured limit in the new window; the behavior does not increase the sustained rate. Stores that return a fresh Date are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 8.7.2.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content.

A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

cna.title: (Simply) Guest Author Name <= 4.42 - Authenticated (Subscriber+) Stored Cross-Site Scripting via Biographical Info

descriptions.value: The (Simply) Guest Author Name plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the user Biographical Info (description) field in versions up to, and including, 4.42. The plugin unconditionally calls remove_filter('pre_user_description', 'wp_filter_kses') at plugin load (sfly-guest-author.php:17), which strips WordPress core's sanitization of the user description field for users who lack the unfiltered_html capability (Subscribers, Contributors, Authors). This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in their own profile Biographical Info that will execute whenever a user accesses a page rendering that author's description (such as an author archive or a single-post author bio in default WordPress themes like Twenty Seventeen and Twenty Fifteen).

cna.title: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js

descriptions.value: Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. From 0.2.0 until 7.1.2, the @astrojs/solid-js renderer inserted a named slot into the quoted name attribute of an astro-slot wrapper without HTML escaping. A request-controlled slot name containing a quote could terminate the attribute and inject active HTML. Exploitation required a hydrated Solid component using a client:* directive and dynamic access to the attacker-chosen slot property; a component that did not render that slot emitted only escaped fallback content. This issue is fixed in version 7.1.2.

cna.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels

descriptions.value: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, the pure-Ruby Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode implementation decodes invalid Punycode A-labels instead of returning them unchanged. Labels that decode to ASCII text or fail to convert back to the same A-label can therefore make Addressable::URI#display_uri show a trusted-looking host while host, normalized_host, and the connection target retain the attacker-controlled encoded host. A trusted-name comparison using Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode output can also treat two different hosts as the same without displaying the URI. The native libidn implementation, to_ascii, and normalized_host are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

cna.title: Loofah allowed_uri? treats javascript&#x3a alert(1) as safe

descriptions.value: Loofah is a general library for manipulating and transforming HTML/XML documents and fragments, built on top of Nokogiri. From 2.25.0 until 2.25.3, Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? strips whitespace and control characters before decoding a semicolon-less numeric character reference, changing where the reference ends and hiding a javascript: or vbscript: scheme that a browser reconstructs. The bypass applies to encoded colons and encoded scheme letters when a stripped character terminates the numeric reference. An application that renders the approved value in href or another browser-interpreted URI attribute can allow cross-site scripting, and Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri? re-exports the affected helper. Loofah's default sanitize() path is not affected because Nokogiri decodes entities before URI evaluation. This issue is fixed in version 2.25.3.

cna.title: Action Mailbox: Possible signature replay in Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress

descriptions.value: Action Mailbox routes incoming emails to controller-like mailboxes for processing in Rails. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress authenticates a request with an HMAC of the timestamp and token parameters concatenated without a separator, and ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::InboundEmailsController::Authenticator#recent? rejects only timestamps more than 2 minutes in the past. Because the signature does not fix the boundary between the two values, a captured signed request can be presented with a timestamp far in the future, which the ingress then accepts indefinitely. An attacker who obtains one signed Mailgun webhook request, but not the signing key, could submit arbitrary inbound email that Action Mailbox processes as genuine, possibly leading to forged messages attributed to the sender of the attacker's choosing. Applications that receive inbound email through the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress are affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Improper Certificate Validation in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, which reads Server= as MariaDB Connector/C does and refuses TlsMode=verify-full with no TlsCaFile before connecting, with HM7535 in the error log, on a connection the client treats as local or a Server= list that holds one, and which says, on such a connection with a TlsCaFile, that the certificate's issuer was checked and not its name. Until then, set TlsCaFile to a file holding only the CA that issues the database server's certificate, at a path in ASCII alone; the client then checks the certificate's issuer on such a connection, though not its name. On these versions the --check-database settings line and the application log say the certificate was checked either way, so they do not show the difference.

descriptions.value: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, TlsMode=verify-full and no TlsCaFile, does not verify the database server's certificate's issuer or name when the connection is one that MariaDB Connector/C treats as local - Server= set to 127.0.0.1, ::1 or localhost (on Linux a Unix socket), to . on Windows (a named pipe), or to a comma-separated list of servers that holds such an element - which allows a local attacker who can stand in for the database server, for example by listening on its port while it is stopped or restarting, to receive the database sign-in, the password included, and to read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database. hMailServer applied verify-full by turning the client's certificate verification on without a CA file, but MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.1 and later, on a connection they treat as local and with no CA file, accept any certificate within its validity period that is self-signed or sent with its own root, for any name (Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 also one whose issuer they cannot find), so the client accepted the certificate an impostor made, asked no proof of the password and allowed a switch to an authentication method that sends the password unhashed, while hmailserver --check-database said the certificate had been checked against the system's trust store and the application log that it had been checked. The Windows builds bundle Connector/C 3.4.9 (6.3.4 to 6.3.6) and 3.4.11 (6.3.7); on Linux the distribution's client is used, and Connector/C 3.3 and 3.4.0 and Oracle's MySQL client are not affected. The configuration is not the default: TlsMode defaults to prefer, which checks no certificate.

cna.title: Awx: webhook credential assignment omits use_role check, exposing another user's token

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Seungwon Kim (0xRrudy) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Grant the Job Template and Workflow Job Template administrator role only to trusted users, and avoid storing webhook token credentials in organizations where untrusted users hold template-admin rights. There is no complete configuration-only mitigation; apply the fix when it becomes available.

descriptions.value: An incorrect authorization flaw was found in AWX, the automation controller component of Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform. The API access classes for JobTemplate and WorkflowJobTemplate do not check the caller's Credential use_role when assigning the single-valued webhook_credential foreign key: JobTemplateAccess.can_add/can_change and WorkflowJobTemplateAccess.can_change in awx/main/access.py omit the check_related('webhook_credential', Credential, ..., role_field='use_role') call that UnifiedCredentialsMixin.can_attach performs for the normal many-to-many credentials relationship, and the serializer validates only the credential's type and namespace. A user who may administer their own job template (or workflow job template) and use its project and inventory can therefore attach a webhook token credential (for example a GitLab token) that they do not have use permission on. The template administrator can retrieve the template's webhook key; a subsequent webhook event causes AWX to decrypt the attached token and send it in the request header (for GitLab, PRIVATE-TOKEN) to a status URL derived from the event payload, disclosing the victim's token to a destination the attacker can influence. This may disclose another user's personal access token and allow whatever actions that token permits.

cna.title: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator

descriptions.value: Soup Sieve is a CSS selector library designed to be used with Beautiful Soup 4. Prior to 4.0, Soup Sieve repeatedly walks the same ancestors while matching descendant combinators, and each additional descendant combinator raises the polynomial degree of the work on deeply nested attacker-influenced HTML or XML. Applications using selectors such as section div div through select(), select_one(), or Beautiful Soup CSS APIs against untrusted documents can have a worker occupied for seconds or minutes, while trusted-only document processing is not affected. Selectors compiled with NOCACHE continue to use the old uncached behavior. This issue is fixed in version 4.0.

cna.title: Ansible.posix: authorized_key module follows a parent-directory symlink allowing writes outside the intended directory

workarounds.value: Do not run ansible.posix.authorized_key as root against home or .ssh directories that unprivileged users can modify. Verify that target directories are not attacker-controllable symlinks before running the task.

descriptions.value: A link-following flaw was found in the authorized_key module of the ansible.posix collection, residual to the fix for CVE-2026-11837. That fix guards only the final path component (os.chown with follow_symlinks=False and O_NOFOLLOW in _safe_open_write()). When an unprivileged local user replaces their ~/.ssh directory with a symlink to a directory they do not own, and an operator subsequently runs the authorized_key task as root (a common provisioning pattern), the module resolves its path operations through the symlink: atomic_move() writes the temporary file in the symlink target and renames it to <target>/authorized_keys, creating or overwriting a file in the attacker-chosen directory, and os.chmod(sshdir, 0o700) follows the symlink and changes the target directory's permissions. The written file is chowned to the unprivileged user, so this is not a privilege escalation, but it allows an attacker to create or overwrite files (for example in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/, which APT reads regardless of file ownership) to cause integrity and availability impacts.

cna.title: Partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution

descriptions.value: CAPEC-586 Object Injection

Partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution.

The files session save handler, which is the default, writes updated session data into the existing session file without first clearing it. If a write is interrupted, the file can contain the beginning of the new session followed by the end of the old one, and bytes of an ordinary string can later be unserialized as objects. An attacker who can influence the session data, for example through session upload progress, and interrupt a write at a suitable point may inject objects, which can lead to code execution when the application contains a suitable gadget chain. Session data can also be corrupted.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

cna.title: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator

descriptions.value: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. From 4.1.4 until 4.13.16, RegExpRouter can omit wildcard middleware in three version-specific cases: since 4.13.0, middleware using the explicit default parameter pattern in /api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/* is not applied to a route written as /api/:tenant/admin/:id; since 4.1.4, middleware on /admin/* is not applied to a route registered as /admin* for paths under /admin/; and since 4.4.0, a request path containing an encoded line terminator can reach the not-found handler without wildcard middleware. The default SmartRouter selects RegExpRouter for most applications, and the router's registration-time coverage calculation treated the first two matching pattern pairs as different while its compiled wildcard did not match line terminators in the third case. An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler or the not-found handler without authentication or authorization middleware registered on the wildcard path. TrieRouter, LinearRouter, and PatternRouter apply the middleware in the three described cases. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

cna.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix

descriptions.value: Hono is a Web application framework that provides support for any JavaScript runtime. Prior to 4.13.16, mount() and app.mount() can remove a dynamic mount prefix using the route-pattern length rather than the matched-prefix length, allowing a crafted path to be forwarded as a protected inner route while the outer application routes the original path. Since 4.12.21, rebuilding the forwarded URL from the decoded pathname can also convert a decoded backslash to a slash and collapse parent-directory segments, again causing the mounted application to receive a protected path. An unauthenticated client can use either applicable path transformation to reach a mounted route without authentication or authorization middleware scoped to a subpath inside the mount prefix. This issue is fixed in version 4.13.16.

cna.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file read and remote code execution in Active Storage video previews, analysis and image processing

descriptions.value: Active Storage makes it simple to upload and reference files in cloud services and attach those files to Active Record objects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, ActiveStorage::Blob#open writes a blob to a tempfile whose name carries the extension of the uploaded filename, and hands that path to ffprobe (VideoAnalyzer, AudioAnalyzer), ffmpeg (VideoPreviewer) and ImageMagick (ImageAnalyzer, the :mini_magick variant processor). These tools select a decoder from the file extension when the content does not identify its own format, so an attacker who chooses the filename and declares the content type of an upload chooses which decoder processes it. An FFmpeg built with AviSynth support treats a file with the .avs extension as an AviSynth script and evaluates it, which could disclose files readable by the application process through the preview image, or load a native library the attacker has also uploaded, possibly leading to remote code execution in the FFmpeg process. ImageMagick selects its coders and delegates from the extension in the same way. An application is affected if it accepts uploads from untrusted users and analyzes video or audio attachments, generates video previews, or processes images with ImageMagick. The AviSynth attack additionally requires an FFmpeg built with --enable-avisynth and the AviSynthPlus runtime on the host. Upstream FFmpeg and the common Linux distribution and Homebrew packages do not enable it; the GPL builds distributed for Windows and Linux from ffmpeg.org do. Other decoders that FFmpeg or ImageMagick select from the extension may be reachable without AviSynth. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: Incorrect Default Permissions in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose setup makes a new program folder, every folder above it that is not there, and Bin and ControlPanel in it, with permissions of their own from the moment each exists - SYSTEM and the Administrators full control, Users read and execute, nothing inherited, the Administrators the owner - before Inno Setup makes a folder or copies a file, each made by its name relative to the folder above it, which setup holds open. Until then, install hMailServer under Program Files, or into a new folder inside a folder that only administrators may change. To install elsewhere, first make the program folder from an elevated Command Prompt and give it a protected set of permissions - icacls "<program folder>" /inheritance:r /grant:r *S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-545:(OI)(CI)RX, then icacls "<program folder>" /setowner *S-1-5-32-544 - check with dir /q /a "<program folder>" that nothing has been made in it, and restart Windows before running setup, so that nothing opened in it before its permissions were set stays open.

descriptions.value: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allow a local authenticated user to run code as the administrator who installs the product, when it is installed into a new program folder in a location whose permissions let every user write, such as the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but its setup lets Inno Setup make a new program folder first, with the permissions the folder above hands down, and replaces them only afterwards, tens of milliseconds later (33 to 139 milliseconds in the project's test runs). In that time any local account may make files and folders in the new folder, which keep that account as their owner, among them the Bin folder that setup then copies the programs into. Setup runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, registering the service among them, before its hardening at the end of setup takes such a folder back, and those programs load a library placed in Bin in place of the system's. The default installation under Program Files, whose folders give ordinary users read and execute only, is not affected.

cna.title: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.4 or later, whose database schema 6102 converts every MySQL and MariaDB table to utf8mb4, and which runs only on a database upgraded to its schema; 6.3.8 also fixes a separate way round the auto-ban. Until then, converting the IP range table as that step does (ALTER TABLE hm_securityranges ENGINE=InnoDB, ROW_FORMAT=DYNAMIC, CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci) lets the database store such a name, and setting MaxInvalidLogonAttempts to 1 closes this way round, since every failed logon then reaches the limit by itself, and a guess at an account, made under a name the table can hold, is banned under it.

descriptions.value: The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.0 through 6.3.3, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords from a single address without being banned. The server makes its MySQL tables in MySQL's utf8 character set, which holds no character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, sends its statements as UTF-8 over a utf8mb4 connection and leaves the database's default strict mode in place. From 6.2.0 it decodes the user name of a SASL PLAIN logon as UTF-8, so the name can hold such a character. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and drops the connection. If such a character is in the part of the user name that the range's name keeps (the name is cut to 100 characters), the database refuses the range: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. An attacker can in this way spend all but the last attempt of each set on password guesses, and make the last under such a name. On Windows, POP3 AUTH PLAIN reaches it on a server as installed, and IMAP AUTHENTICATE PLAIN where IMAP SASL authentication is turned on (off by default); on Windows and on Linux (from 6.3.0), SMTP AUTH PLAIN reaches it where plain-text authentication is allowed (off by default), and ManageSieve and CardDAV where they are turned on (off by default). Each failed save is reported in the server's error log. A database whose strict mode has been turned off stores the character as a question mark and makes the first such ban, but refuses every later ban named after the same user name, or after one holding other such characters in their place, as a duplicate while the first stands, since the server cannot look up a name holding such a character there.

credits.value: This issue was discovered by Elijah DeLee (Red Hat Inc.).

descriptions.value: A cleartext storage flaw was found in the AAP Gateway Operator. When reconciling an AutomationController, the operator reads the protected resource-server Secret (Secret/<aap-name>-resource-server, key controller_resource_server_secret) and copies its plaintext value into the generated AutomationController custom resource under spec.extra_settings (RESOURCE_SERVER.SECRET_KEY). Although the operator uses no_log to keep the value out of its own logs, serializing it into the custom resource exposes it to any principal able to read the AutomationController CR without permission to read the backing Kubernetes Secret, breaking the expected OpenShift RBAC separation between the two resources. The value may also propagate into Kubernetes API/etcd storage, GitOps and Argo diffs and history, rendered manifests, support bundles, and audit data. The resource-server secret is intended for trusted Gateway-to-Controller service authentication, and its disclosure may allow a user to impersonate a trusted Controller service and reach privileged service-index APIs.

cna.title: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism in hMailServer

credits.value: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

solutions.value: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, in which a failed sign-in at the web services listener from loopback or from an address in WebServicesTrustedProxies is counted against the user name alone, towards the per-name lockout (AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default), and never towards a ban of the address, as for an address in AutoBanNeverBan; a failure from any other address counts as before. A proxy at another address that is not listed, forwarding to the HTTPS port, is not taken for a proxy and is charged as before, as a load balancer is at the mail listeners, until its address is in WebServicesTrustedProxies; from 6.3.8 a ban its clients earn also closes the web services listener to it. Through a proxy the per-name lockout is then the limit on the guesses at one account, so turn it on there. Until then, put the proxy's address in AutoBanNeverBan (127.0.0.1 and ::1 for a proxy on the same machine), which keeps the auto-ban from counting that address's failed logons on any protocol; turning the auto-ban on failed logons off, or setting MaxInvalidLogonAttempts or AutoBanMinutes to 0, also avoids it, for every address. From 6.3.6 the never-ban list by reverse name spares a proxy at another address whose forward-confirmed reverse name it covers, lifting the ban once the name is confirmed; it cannot name loopback.

descriptions.value: The web services listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.3 through 6.3.7 counts every failed CardDAV, CalDAV or Autodiscover sign-in from a proxy it trusts - one on the same machine, or one named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, whose X-Forwarded-Proto it believes - against the proxy's own address, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach the proxy to have that address banned from the server's mail listeners. The listener, off by default (WebServicesHttpPort and WebServicesHttpsPort 0), signs an account in with HTTP Basic over HTTPS for CardDAV from 6.3.3 and for CalDAV and Outlook Autodiscover from 6.3.4. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, which the server trusts when it is on the same machine or named in WebServicesTrustedProxies, the listener takes the client's HTTPS from the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header, but it does not believe X-Forwarded-For and sees the proxy's address for every client. Each failed sign-in counted towards the auto-ban against that address, so that failed sign-ins through the proxy from anybody, under any user name, reaching MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 within 30 minutes by default) wrote an IP range that refused the proxy's address at the SMTP, POP3, IMAP and ManageSieve listeners for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default), and could write it again each time it lapsed. For a proxy on the same machine that address is the loopback address, so that a webmail on that machine, local scripts that submit mail and the other local clients of the mail listeners were shut out; for a proxy at another address that also carries mail, every mail client behind it was. Such a proxy forwarding to the listener's HTTPS port, re-encrypting, was counted against in the same way, and listing it in WebServicesTrustedProxies did not spare it. The auto-ban is on by default and AutoBanNeverBan, which spares an address, is empty by default; the listener itself went on serving the proxy.

descriptions.description: CWE-645: Overly Restrictive Account Lockout Mechanism

cna.title: Ansible-pylibssh: accepts a changed ssh host key when host_key_auto_add is enabled

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Satriyo Utomo (aleens-labs) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Do not enable host_key_auto_add (ansible.netcommon libssh) or AutoAddPolicy (ansible-pylibssh). Keep host_key_checking enabled and pre-populate known_hosts with verified host keys so that a changed key causes the connection to fail closed.

descriptions.value: A host key verification flaw was found in ansible-pylibssh and in the ansible.netcommon libssh connection plugin. When trust-on-first-use is enabled (host_key_auto_add on the libssh connection plugin, or AutoAddPolicy in ansible-pylibssh), a host that is already present in known_hosts but now presents a different key is accepted without warning. The pylibssh Session.verify_knownhost() method passes the SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS_CHANGED and SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS_OTHER states to the same missing_host_key() policy hook used for unknown hosts, and the bundled AutoAddPolicy/RejectPolicy classes (as well as ansible.netcommon's MyAddPolicy, which is modeled on paramiko's AutoAddPolicy) therefore add the changed key and continue the connection rather than aborting as paramiko's BadHostKeyException path would. As a result the controller authenticates to the substitute host, runs the play there, and appends the new key to known_hosts, which can disclose connection credentials to an attacker performing a machine-in-the-middle attack. Default configurations (host_key_checking enabled, host_key_auto_add unset) are not affected; non-interactive runs fail closed.

cna.title: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in Active Storage GCS direct uploads with cache_control

descriptions.value: Active Storage makes it simple to upload and reference files in cloud services and attach those files to Active Record objects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, when a GCS service is configured with the cache_control option, ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the Cache-Control and Host headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a Content-Type of its choosing, and can omit the declared Content-MD5, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the response-content-type that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on storage.googleapis.com. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket. Applications that use the GCS service with cache_control configured and accept direct uploads are affected. GCS services without cache_control sign with V2 and are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.

cna.title: OpenObserve: Empty external password allows authentication bypass

descriptions.value: OpenObserve is a cloud-native observability platform. Prior to 1.1.0, the shared authentication validator in src/api/common/src/auth/validator.rs accepts an empty or whitespace-only HTTP Basic password for an account whose password_ext value is missing or empty. SSO-provisioned and migration-created users can have this state, allowing an unauthenticated attacker who knows an affected user's email address and organization to authenticate on protected non-ingestion API routes with the victim's role and permissions. A compromised privileged account can expose or modify telemetry, alerts, streams, users, and security configuration. An account with search permission can submit a DataFusion COPY ... TO statement through the search API to create or overwrite attacker-controlled files at service-process-writable locations, creating a conditional escalation to pre-authentication remote code execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.1.0.

cna.title: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation

descriptions.value: @grpc/grpc-js implements the core functionality of gRPC purely in JavaScript, without a C++ addon. Before 1.13.2, and from 1.14.0 through 1.14.1, the @grpc/grpc-js-xds SafeRegexValueMatcher and PathSafeRegexValueMatcher add start and end anchors without grouping a supplied top-level alternation. An expression intended to match one of several complete values can therefore match a prefix, substring, or suffix. The affected matchers are used for route selection, xDS credential identity matching, and RBAC URL path, principal name, server name, and header rules. An ALLOW policy using an alternation can consequently accept a method, certificate identity, or header value outside the intended set, while a DENY policy becomes broader rather than permissive. This issue is fixed in versions 1.13.2 and 1.14.2.

descriptions.value: A deserialization type-restriction control in the BSON serialization component can be bypassed because the check used to recognize a class of compiler-generated types relies on an overly permissive heuristic rather than a precise identification. An unauthorized party able to supply BSON content that an application later deserializes into a loosely typed member can cause types outside the intended allow-list to be constructed and populated with unauthorized party-supplied values inside the consuming application. This can lead to unexpected object state and errors in downstream application logic. No elevated privileges beyond the ability to place unauthorized party-influenced content in the deserialization path are required.

cna.title: Active Support: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize

descriptions.value: Active Support is a collection of utility classes and standard library extensions used by Rails and other Ruby projects. Prior to 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2, when constant lookup raises LoadError, ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize (and String#safe_constantize) builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application unavailable. Action Cable passes the channel value of each subscribe command to safe_constantize before any channel lookup, so an unauthenticated client can reach this code when the application mounts Action Cable and accepts connections from untrusted clients without an added authentication check. This issue is fixed in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2.
