patches.subject: fix: [security] Create the installer log and its FIFO

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Create the installer log and its FIFO
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The installer scripts now explicitly create the log file with 0600 permissions using install -m 0600 and the FIFO with mkfifo -m 0600, ensuring both are root-readable/writable only from the moment of creation. The log file is also removed (rm -f) before creation to prevent a pre-existing symlink in /var/log from being used to redirect the write to an attacker-controlled path. This matches the existing 0600 treatment applied to /root/misp_settings.txt by the save_settings() function.
assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the tag_version_boundary (v2.5.47 with 38 commits after fix); the exact first affected version is not specified in the patch metadata.

The vulnerability is transient in the sense that it only manifests during the installer execution window, but the log file persists on disk after installation and remains world-readable unless the administrator manually changes permissions or removes it.

The CVSS assumes the log file remains on disk after installation; if it is immediately removed by the installer, the exposure window is shorter but the file is still readable during the installation process.
CAPEC-135 is the closest available attack pattern; no CAPEC specifically covers 'reading a world-readable log file containing credentials,' so the general permission-misuse pattern is the best match.
The symlink attack vector (CWE-22) is a secondary concern addressed by the same patch; the primary vulnerability is the incorrect file permissions (CWE-732).
The installer is assumed to run as root (standard for system installation scripts), which is why 0600 permissions restrict access to root only.

The subsequent tee and exec redirection lines remain unchanged.

cna.title: MISP: Disabled-user check ineffective in pre-authentication TOTP login branch

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [login] Fetch User.disabled in the pre-auth TOTP lookup

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [login] Fetch User.disabled in the pre-auth TOTP lookup
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix adds User.disabled to the fields array of the pre-authentication find() query so that the disabled-user check in the TOTP branch reads the actual column value and correctly rejects disabled users before they reach the TOTP verification step, restoring the intended guard behavior.
assumptions: The commit message states the issue is 'harmless in practice' because identify() re-checks the user; this advisory treats the security impact as minimal (minor information disclosure only).

The TOTP feature was introduced in 2023 per the commit message; the exact affected version range is not specified in the patch. The tag boundary v2.5.47 is used as an upper bound for the affected range but is not confirmed as the exact fixed version.
CAPEC-1 (Brute Force) is the closest available attack pattern; the actual scenario is a minor authentication-guard bypass rather than a full brute-force attack, so the mapping is approximate.

CVSS VC:L is assigned for the marginal information-disclosure difference in the login response; if the CNA determines no meaningful confidentiality impact exists, VC:N would be more appropriate, resulting in a score of 0.0.

The PHP version behavior (Warning vs Notice vs Error for undefined array keys) may vary, but in all supported PHP versions the code continues execution with a null value, so the security analysis is unaffected.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: A single-line change in app/Controller/UsersController.php appends 'User.disabled' to the fields list of the pre-authentication User find() query in the login() method (line 1385), ensuring the disabled flag is present in the result set when the TOTP branch evaluates it.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: The vulnerability is reachable over the network (AV:N) via the web login endpoint with low complexity (AC:L), no attack target (AT:N), no prior privileges (PR:N), and no user interaction (UI:N). The only potential impact is a very minor confidentiality difference: a disabled, TOTP-enrolled user receives a TOTP prompt instead of an immediate rejection, which could marginally aid account-status enumeration (VC:L). There is no integrity or availability impact (VI:N, VA:N) and no secondary impacts (SC:N, SI:N, SA:N) because the subsequent identify() call still enforces the disabled-user check. The commit message explicitly characterizes the issue as 'harmless in practice.'

capecRationale.rationale: The closest plausible CAPEC is Brute Force, as the scenario involves an attacker attempting to authenticate using known credentials of a disabled, TOTP-enrolled account. The disabled-user guard that should have blocked the attempt at the TOTP branch was ineffective, allowing the attempt to proceed one step further than intended. This mapping is uncertain because the vulnerability does not enable a full authentication bypass (identify() still rejects the user) and the primary effect is a minor information-disclosure difference in the login response rather than a successful brute-force attack.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The disabled-user check in the TOTP login branch was ineffective because the required column was not fetched, allowing a disabled user to pass that guard. The subsequent identify() call still enforced the check, limiting the impact. CWE-285 is the narrowest defensible mapping for an authentication-state check that does not function as intended.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-1 Brute Force

solutions.value: The fix adds User.disabled to the fields array of the pre-authentication find() query so that the disabled-user check in the TOTP branch reads the actual column value and correctly rejects disabled users before they reach the TOTP verification step, restoring the intended guard behavior.

supportingMedia.value: The fix adds User.disabled to the fields array of the pre-authentication find() query so that the disabled-user check in the TOTP branch reads the actual column value and correctly rejects disabled users before they reach the TOTP verification step, restoring the intended guard behavior.

descriptions.value:
In MISP's UsersController login() method, the pre-authentication database query used for the TOTP (two-factor authentication) verification branch did not include the User.disabled column in its SELECT fields list. The query selected only User.password, User.totp, and User.hotp_counter. When the TOTP branch subsequently accessed $unauth_user['User']['disabled'], the key was absent from the result set, producing a PHP 'Undefined array key' warning and causing the expression to evaluate as null (falsy). As a result, the disabled-user guard in the TOTP branch was effectively a no-op: a disabled, TOTP-enrolled user could proceed to the TOTP verification step rather than being rejected at that point. 

The commit message explicitly states this was 'harmless in practice' because the subsequent identify() call re-validates the user and would still reject a disabled account. 

The practical security impact is therefore minimal, limited to a very small information-disclosure difference in the login response (a TOTP prompt is presented instead of an immediate rejection) and a PHP warning in application logs.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Harden misp modules module choice
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix adds a moduleFound flag that is set only when the requested module name matches an entry in the enabled modules list. After the lookup loop completes, if the flag remains false, the method throws a MethodNotAllowedException with the message 'Module not found or not available,' effectively rejecting any query that references a module not present in the enabled set.
assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the tag_version_boundary (v2.5.47 with 138 commits after fix); the exact last affected version and first fixed version are not explicitly stated in the patch metadata.
The security impact is assessed as low confidentiality impact based on the limited evidence; the actual data exposure depends on what legacy modules would process, which is not detailed in the patch.

CAPEC-124 (Parameter Tampering) is the closest available attack pattern; the actual scenario is a server-side input validation gap rather than an active tampering attack, so the mapping is approximate.

The patch does not specify whether the legacy module query could lead to code execution, data exfiltration, or other higher-impact consequences; the CVSS impact metrics are conservatively set to reflect only the evidenced behavior.
Authentication is assumed to be required (PR:L) based on MISP being an authenticated web application; the patch does not explicitly state authentication requirements.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Controller/EventsController.php, the queryEnrichment method is modified: a boolean variable $moduleFound is initialized to false before the foreach loop over $enabledModules['modules']. Inside the loop, when a module name matches, $moduleFound is set to true. After the loop, a new conditional block checks if $moduleFound is still false and throws a MethodNotAllowedException, preventing further processing with an unavailable module.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: The vulnerability is exploitable over the network (AV:N) via the MISP web interface with low complexity (AC:L) and no attack target manipulation (AT:N). It requires a low-privilege authenticated user (PR:L) and no user interaction (UI:N). The primary impact is a low confidentiality impact (VC:L) because an authenticated user could trigger processing through a module not in the enabled set, potentially exposing data or processing results not intended to be available. No integrity or availability impact is evidenced (VI:N, VA:N). No secondary impacts are indicated (SC:N, SI:N, SA:N). The low impact reflects that the user already has authenticated access to the event and the exposure is limited to an additional module processing path.

capecRationale.rationale: The closest plausible attack pattern is parameter tampering: an authenticated user supplies a module name in the queryEnrichment request that is not in the enabled modules list (e.g., a legacy or disabled module). The server previously accepted this parameter value and processed the request with defaults. The uncertainty is that the patch does not explicitly describe an active tampering scenario; it is a server-side validation gap. CAPEC-124 is selected as the best available match because the core mechanism is the manipulation of a request parameter to reference an unauthorized resource.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The module name parameter supplied to queryEnrichment was not validated against the set of enabled/available modules. The code accepted any module name and, when no match was found, proceeded with default parameters instead of rejecting the input. The fix adds an explicit validation check that rejects the request when the module is not in the enabled list.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-124 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix adds a moduleFound flag that is set only when the requested module name matches an entry in the enabled modules list. After the lookup loop completes, if the flag remains false, the method throws a MethodNotAllowedException with the message 'Module not found or not available,' effectively rejecting any query that references a module not present in the enabled set.

descriptions.value: In MISP, the queryEnrichment method in EventsController.php accepted a module name parameter and iterated over the list of enabled modules to find a match. If the specified module was not present in the enabled modules list, the code silently continued processing using default parameters (format set to 'simplified' and no module-specific configuration applied) rather than rejecting the request. descriptions.value:
MISP contains a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the event REST search export confirmation form. The view template app/View/Events/ajax/eventRestSearchExportConfirmationForm.ctp renders a URL-supplied event ID list into a single-quoted JavaScript string literal using PHP's json_encode() without any hex-encoding flags. By default, json_encode() escapes double quotes and backslashes but does not escape single quotes. Because the JavaScript string is delimited by single quotes, an attacker can inject a single-quote character to terminate the string literal and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session.

The vulnerability affects the Default and UiBeta themes, both of which render this view. The Overmind theme's own copy of the form already passed the value through an escaped data attribute and was not affected by this specific sink.

Preconditions: the victim must be an authenticated MISP user and must actively open or navigate to the attacker-crafted URL. The attacker does not require an account or any prior access to the MISP instance.

Security impact: successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the MISP web application, potentially leading to session hijacking, unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim, exfiltration of sensitive data visible in the session, or further client-side attacks. The vulnerable component's own confidentiality, integrity, and availability are not directly compromised; the impact is on the underlying user session.

cna.title: Out-of-Bounds Read and Incorrect IV Length Handling in AES-GCM-SIV

descriptions.value:
Issue summary: Setting an AES-GCM-SIV IV shorter than the expected nonce
length via EVP_CipherInit_ex() may trigger a heap out-of-bounds read.
Supplying a longer IV is silently truncated instead of rejected.

Impact summary: An application passing a caller-supplied IV of the wrong
length may crash or read beyond its buffer. Because trailing IV bytes are
ignored, an attacker who knows one message and tag may forge messages under a
different IV.

CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read

Description: AES-GCM-SIV copies the caller-supplied IV or nonce into its
internal state using a copy whose length is taken from the expected nonce size
rather than from the length the caller actually provided. When the caller
passes a shorter IV, the copy reads past the end of the caller's buffer;
AddressSanitizer confirms a heap out-of-bounds read reached through
EVP_CipherInit_ex() into ossl_aes_gcm_siv_init(). When the caller passes a
longer IV, the implementation silently discards the trailing bytes instead of
rejecting the length.

The truncation breaks the binding between the IV and the computed
authentication tag. An attacker who has observed a message and its tag under
one IV can produce a message and tag that verify under a different IV whose
first bytes match, since the surplus bytes never influence the computation.
The message itself is unchanged, so this is a failure of IV commitment rather
than a classic existential forgery.

Only applications that call EVP_CipherInit_ex() (or the equivalent provider
cipher initialization) with an IV length other than the standard 12 bytes for
AES-GCM-SIV are affected. The severity is limited because the out-of-bounds
read is small and attacker-controlled only in length, and the forgery requires
an unusual IV length choice by the application.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS modules are not affected by this issue, as AES-GCM-SIV is not an
approved algorithm.

cna.title: AT_SECURE program buffer overflow via $ORIGIN processing

credits.value: AISLE in partnership with Red Hat

descriptions.value: CAPEC-100 Overflow Buffers

A stack-based buffer overflow in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to crash or corrupt the memory of setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs.

When such a program's DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN and is followed by NUL or '/' the loader both reads past the end of the path buffer and writes past the end of a stack-allocated internal buffer. The corrupted loader stack can lead to a loader crash (denial of service) and limited disclosure of process memory.

references.name: Move allowDowngrades from the check command to the plugin configuration

descriptions.value: The Tauri updater plugin's 'check' IPC command accepts an allowDowngrades boolean parameter directly from frontend JavaScript code. When set to true, it replaces the version comparator from "update must be newer" to "update must be different." Because the default permission set grants allow-check to the webview, any XSS in the app frontend can invoke this command and bypass the only anti-rollback protection the updater offers. Combined with another bug, this enables downgrade attacks without even needing to fake a higher version number.

descriptions.value: A heap-based buffer overflow flaw was found in rpm. Parsing a symlink entry in an untrusted RPM package whose declared RPMTAG_LONGFILESIZES value is 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF causes an integer overflow in iterReadArchiveNext() that shrinks a buffer allocation to one byte, after which the payload's independently-controlled cpio filesize field is used to write attacker-controlled data past the end of that allocation. cna.title: Cortex-A7 module data validation checks only the first address of a caller-supplied range

descriptions.value:
The Cortex-A7 MMU Modules port validates a caller-supplied buffer by translating **one address** — the first byte. The common Module Manager hands its range check the module instance, the start address and the complete byte size; the Cortex-A7 implementation discarded the instance and the size and asked the MMU a single question about the start.



A memory-protected module therefore passed any range whose first byte was user-readable, however far the rest of it reached. Privileged dispatch code then read or wrote the whole range. Because every protected-module dispatcher that consumes a buffer or an extra-parameter array goes through this one macro, the defect is not in any individual service: it is in the primitive all of them rely on.

cna.title: Use-after-free and net_buf leak in Zephyr TCP header linearization (tcp_pkt_linearize)

descriptions.value:
tcp_pkt_linearize() in subsys/net/ip/tcp.c is used by th_get() whenever a received TCP header is not contiguous in a single net_buf. While pulling the header bytes out of the following fragments, the loop called net_buf_unref() on an emptied fragment without first detaching its frags pointer. net_buf_unref() walks the whole fragment list, so the payload buffers still linked behind that fragment were freed as well, and the stale pointer was then reinstalled into the packet as buf->frags, producing a use-after-free and a later double free during packet teardown. The same loop also advanced to second->frags unconditionally: when the fragment still held payload after the header remainder was pulled, it was spliced out of the packet without ever being unreferenced, permanently leaking that buffer and silently dropping the data it carried.

The defect is reached from tcp_recv() via th_get() on every received TCP segment, before connection lookup or any header validation, so a single unauthenticated segment that matches a listening socket is sufficient. An attacker only needs the TCP header to straddle a net_buf boundary, which they can arrange from off-link: IPv6 extension headers are accepted on receive and their length is added to the header offset by th_get(), so a Destination Options header of a suitable length places the TCP header across the boundary of the fixed-size receive buffers (CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE). Packet chains assembled from several sources - IPv4/IPv6 reassembly, 6LoWPAN/802.15.4 reassembly, tunnel or virtual interfaces that strip an outer header, or drivers producing scatter-gather chains - can additionally present a short interior fragment that the loop empties exactly, which is the case that frees the remainder of the packet while it is still in use.

The reliably reachable consequence is exhaustion of the receive buffer pool: each crafted segment leaks one net_buf from the fixed CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT pool, the buffers are never reclaimed, and once the pool is empty the device can no longer receive network traffic until it is rebooted. Where a fragment is emptied exactly, the impact rises to memory corruption: freed pool buffers are written through by the remainder of the loop, their contents may be delivered to the application, and the packet is double-freed on teardown.

The fix saves and clears second->frags before the net_buf_unref() so only the emptied header fragment is released, and advances to the next fragment only when second->len == 0, keeping any fragment that still holds payload in the packet. This restores the detach-before-unref ownership pattern used elsewhere in the stack, for example in net_pkt_trim_buffer().

cna.title: Moquette unbounded per-session message queues allow memory exhaustion

cna.title: Out-of-bounds read and kernel stack disclosure in the SOCKS5 client when the destination address family differs from the proxy address family

descriptions.value:
The SOCKS5 client in subsys/net/lib/socks/socks.c built the CONNECT request in socks5_tcp_connect() by choosing the SOCKS5 address type from the address family of the proxy (proxy->sa_family) while reading the bytes out of the destination address supplied to connect(). A SOCKS5 request encodes the destination independently of the transport used to reach the proxy, so the two families are unrelated and nothing in the path forces them to agree: set_context_proxy() only requires the proxy family to match the socket, and zsock_connect_ctx() enters the SOCKS branch before any destination validation. With an IPv6 proxy and an AF_INET destination the code treated an 8-byte struct net_sockaddr_in as a struct net_sockaddr_in6 and copied the 16-byte sin6_addr from it, reading 12 bytes past the end of the object and transmitting them to the proxy.

With CONFIG_USERSPACE enabled, z_vrfy_zsock_connect() copies only addrlen user bytes into a stack-resident struct net_sockaddr_storage and enforces no per-family minimum length, so the oversized read stays within the storage but returns stale, uninitialised kernel-stack bytes. An unprivileged user-mode thread can therefore open an AF_INET6 stream socket, point setsockopt(SO_SOCKS5) at a proxy it controls, and call connect() with a short AF_INET destination to have the kernel send it 12 bytes of supervisor stack residue per attempt. Without CONFIG_USERSPACE the read runs past the end of the caller's own struct net_sockaddr_in, disclosing adjacent memory to the proxy; the family mismatch can arise unintentionally when a destination is obtained from DNS while an IPv6 proxy is configured.

Impact is limited to information disclosure of at most 12 bytes per connect() call, with no write primitive; the leak is delivered to whoever operates the SOCKS5 proxy. The mirrored pairing (IPv6 destination through an IPv4 proxy) is memory-safe but encoded the destination as SOCKS5_ATYP_IPV4 from the first four bytes of the IPv6 address, causing the proxy to connect to an unrelated host. Exploitation requires the non-default CONFIG_SOCKS option, a socket with SO_SOCKS5 configured, and both IPv4 and IPv6 support in the image.

The fix moves the encoding into a helper that selects the address type from dest->sa_family and validates dest_len against the matching struct net_sockaddr_in/struct net_sockaddr_in6 before copying, rejecting under-length or unsupported destinations with an error.

cna.title: Themify Builder <= 7.8.1 - Unauthenticated Stored Cross-Site Scripting via 'css[fonts]' Parameter

descriptions.value: The Themify Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via 'css[fonts]' Parameter in all versions up to, and including, 7.8.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The nonce required to reach the vulnerable endpoint is embedded in plain sight within the front-end page markup for all visitors, reducing the access control to a CSRF token rather than an authentication barrier and making the endpoint fully exploitable by unauthenticated attackers.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Keep the CSRF check on stateless workflow

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Keep the CSRF check on stateless workflow
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The moduleStatelessExecution action is removed from the unlockedActions list, restoring the CSRF token check. A new mechanism (_csrfTokenHeaderOnly) is introduced that enforces the CSRF token while exempting only the field hash, which the legitimate caller (the module dialog) cannot produce because it posts a hand-built object. The module dialog's AJAX request is updated to send the CSRF token in the X-CSRF-Token header, satisfying the token check without requiring a field hash.
assumptions: The affected version range is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.47, 6 commits after fix), implying the fix is included in v2.5.47 and prior versions are affected. The exact introduction version of the vulnerable code is unknown.

UI:A is used because the CSRF attack requires the victim to actively navigate to the attacker's page or click a link; a purely passive load (e.g., embedded iframe auto-submit) would map to UI:P, but the commit message describes a 'cross-site form post' which typically requires at least a page visit.
SI:N is chosen because the evidence only demonstrates integrity impact on MISP's own blocklist and warninglist data; no evidence supports impact on downstream or external systems.
The CAPEC-124 mapping is confident based on the explicit description of a cross-site form post in the commit message.
The commit message states the issue was 'found during the internal review, not externally reported,' but does not explicitly name a finder; therefore no finder credit is assigned.

The _csrfTokenHeaderOnly method is referenced in the patch but its implementation is not shown; it is assumed to enforce CSRF token validation while exempting the field hash, as described in the commit message.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In WorkflowsController::beforeFilter(), the line adding 'moduleStatelessExecution' to $this->Security->unlockedActions is replaced with a call to $this->_csrfTokenHeaderOnly(['moduleStatelessExecution']), which enforces CSRF token validation while waiving only the field hash requirement. In execute_module.ctp, the jQuery $.ajax() call is modified to include the header 'X-CSRF-Token' populated from window.csrfToken, so the legitimate client-side caller passes the token check via the header rather than a form field.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The attack is delivered over the network via a malicious web page. AC:L: Crafting a cross-site form post is straightforward. AT:N: No special conditions or timing are required. PR:N: The attacker requires no account or privileges on the MISP instance. UI:A: The victim (a site admin) must actively visit the attacker-controlled page or click a link that triggers the form submission. VC:N: No confidentiality impact is evident. VI:H: The attacker can write arbitrary blocklist and warninglist entries, significantly compromising the integrity of MISP's security data. VA:N: No availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N: No evidence of impact on other systems beyond MISP itself.

capecRationale.rationale: The attack pattern described in the commit message is a cross-site form post that causes an authenticated site admin to execute a workflow module with attacker-chosen parameters. This maps directly to CAPEC-124, which describes an attacker exploiting the trust a web application places in a user's browser session to perform unauthorized actions. The mapping is confident because the commit message explicitly describes a cross-site form post bypassing CSRF protection.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The vulnerable action was placed in unlockedActions, which disabled the CSRF token check. This allowed a cross-site form post to trigger a state-changing action (workflow module execution) on behalf of an authenticated administrator, which is the textbook definition of CSRF.

solutions.value: The moduleStatelessExecution action is removed from the unlockedActions list, restoring the CSRF token check. A new mechanism (_csrfTokenHeaderOnly) is introduced that enforces the CSRF token while exempting only the field hash, which the legitimate caller (the module dialog) cannot produce because it posts a hand-built object. The module dialog's AJAX request is updated to send the CSRF token in the X-CSRF-Token header, satisfying the token check without requiring a field hash.

descriptions.value:
MISP's WorkflowsController exposed the moduleStatelessExecution action in the Security component's unlockedActions list. In CakePHP, listing an action in unlockedActions disables both the CSRF token check and the field hash validation for that action. Because moduleStatelessExecution executes a workflow module's exec() method with caller-supplied input and parameters, the absence of CSRF protection allowed an attacker to craft a cross-site form post (or equivalent cross-origin request) that, when submitted by an authenticated site administrator, would cause the administrator's browser to invoke the action on the MISP instance. 

The attacker could select any workflow module to execute, including action modules that write blocklist and warninglist entries, and supply arbitrary input and parameters of their choosing. This constitutes a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability with high integrity impact on the MISP instance's security-related data. 

The vulnerability was identified during an internal security review and was not externally reported. The fix is included in MISP v2.5.47.

cna.title: MISP Reflected Cross-Site Scripting in Attribute Histogram via Unescaped URL-Supplied Type List

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [security] Escape the selected types in the attribute

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [security] Escape the selected types in the attribute
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix replaces the unsafe raw PHP loop that concatenated type values into a JavaScript array literal with a call to json_encode() using the JSON_HEX_TAG, JSON_HEX_APOS, JSON_HEX_QUOT, and JSON_HEX_AMP flags. This ensures that all special characters (angle brackets, quotes, ampersands) in the type values are hex-encoded, preventing any value from breaking out of the JavaScript string/array context and injecting arbitrary script.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.47 with 46 commits after the fix); the exact first affected version is not stated in the patch and is assumed to be all versions prior to the fix commit.

The UI:A (Active) rating assumes the victim must click a link or manually navigate to the crafted URL; if the URL could be triggered via an auto-redirect or embedded iframe, UI:P (Passive) might be more appropriate.

SC:L and SI:L are conservative ratings for the secondary-system impact; a full session hijack or data exfiltration could justify SC:H/SI:H, but the patch evidence does not specify the exact scope of exploitable data.
The CAPEC-1 mapping is the closest available pattern; no CAPEC sub-pattern specifically covers reflected XSS in inline JavaScript event handlers, so the general XSS pattern is used.
The commit message references 'any logged-in victim,' implying authentication is required; the exact role or permission level of the victim is not specified.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/View/Elements/histogram.ctp, the onClick attribute previously built a JS array by iterating over $selectedTypes and echoing each value between double quotes with no escaping: [<?php foreach ($selectedTypes as $t) echo '"' . $t . '", ' ?>]. The patch replaces this with a single json_encode($selectedTypes, JSON_HEX_TAG | JSON_HEX_APOS | JSON_HEX_QUOT | JSON_HEX_AMP) call, producing a safely encoded JSON array literal that cannot be broken out of by any element value.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The vulnerability is exploitable over the network via a crafted URL. AC:L: No race conditions or special environment conditions are required; the attacker simply crafts a URL with a malicious type value. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is needed. PR:N: The attacker requires no privileges on the MISP instance; the victim must be authenticated, but that is a precondition on the victim, not a privilege requirement on the attacker. UI:A: The victim must actively click a link or navigate to the attacker-supplied URL for the reflected payload to execute. VC:N, VI:N, VA:N: The MISP server itself is not directly compromised; the impact is confined to the victim's browser session. SC:L: The attacker can read session tokens or data visible in the MISP UI within the victim's browser. SI:L: The attacker can perform actions on behalf of the victim within the MISP application. SA:N: No availability impact on the victim's browser or the MISP server.

capecRationale.rationale: CAPEC-1 is the canonical CAPEC pattern for cross-site scripting attacks, covering reflected, stored, and DOM-based variants. The patch evidence shows a reflected XSS where URL-supplied data is injected into an inline JavaScript event handler. CAPEC-1 is the closest and most direct match. No more specific CAPEC sub-pattern for reflected XSS in inline JS handlers exists in the CAPEC catalog, so CAPEC-1 is the best available mapping.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The patch directly addresses the reflection of untrusted, URL-supplied data into a JavaScript context within an HTML attribute without encoding. This is a textbook reflected XSS (CWE-79). The specific sub-type is reflected XSS in a JavaScript context (inline event handler), but CWE-79 is the standard and most precise mapping.

solutions.value: The fix replaces the unsafe raw PHP loop that concatenated type values into a JavaScript array literal with a call to json_encode() using the JSON_HEX_TAG, JSON_HEX_APOS, JSON_HEX_QUOT, and JSON_HEX_AMP flags. This ensures that all special characters (angle brackets, quotes, ampersands) in the type values are hex-encoded, preventing any value from breaking out of the JavaScript string/array context and injecting arbitrary script.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the attribute histogram view. The $selectedTypes variable, which is derived from the URL path segment , was interpolated directly into a JavaScript array literal inside an onClick HTML attribute without any encoding or escaping. An attacker who can cause an authenticated MISP user to visit a crafted URL containing a malicious type value can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser within the MISP application origin.

Successful exploitation allows the attacker to read session cookies, perform actions on behalf of the victim, or exfiltrate sensitive data accessible from the MISP interface. 

The vulnerability requires the victim to be authenticated and to actively navigate to the attacker-supplied URL.

cna.title: Excessive Memory Allocation in DTLS Handshake Message Reassembly

descriptions.value:
Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may
cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each
buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of
memory.

Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake
fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of
memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of
Service if many connections are made.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented,
so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until
reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives,
OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the
fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes
actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate
list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message
type rather than only to Certificate messages.

Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not
use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large
message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message
sequence numbers.

A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156
bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory
exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity
is Low.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

cna.title: @fastify/reply-from vulnerable to path traversal via backslash dot-segment prefix escape

descriptions.value: @fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions up to and including 12.8.0, the plugin validated proxy paths against forward-slash dot-segments only and then built the target with the WHATWG URL parser, which normalizes a backslash and its percent-encoded form to a forward slash on the http, https, ws, and wss schemes. A path that uses backslash dot-segments therefore bypasses the traversal check and resolves to a different upstream path, so an application that scopes proxying to an upstream prefix, or relies on route guards in front of the forwarding call, can have an unauthenticated request escape the intended prefix and reach other upstream endpoints. The resulting access to unintended upstream resources is primarily a confidentiality impact with limited integrity impact. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.1, where the path is normalized and any segment resolving to a single or double dot, along with control characters and ambiguous whitespace, is rejected before the URL is constructed, and users should upgrade to 12.8.1 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading.

descriptions.value:
Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions vulnerability in the pattern and patternProperties keywords in lud jsv allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass schema validation via a string that matches a schema regex only after heavy backtracking. JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2 runs schema regexes with a backtracking budget but calls :re.run/3 without :report_errors, so a match that exhausts the budget returns the same :nomatch as a real non-match. A key that matches a patternProperties regex is then checked against additionalProperties or not at all, and a string that matches a not subschema with a pattern is accepted. Before the budget existed, Regex.match?/2 failed the same way at Erlang's default match limit.

Only schemas whose regex explores a catastrophic branch before the branch that matches are affected. The attacker controls the data, not the schema, and linear patterns never exhaust the budget.

This issue affects jsv: from 0.1.0 before 0.26.2.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Bounded matching. JSV.Helpers.RegexExt.bounded_match?/2 in lib/jsv/helpers/regex_ext.ex runs each schema regex through :re.run/3 with match_limit and match_limit_recursion set to 10_000 + 50 * byte_size(subject), capped at 10,000,000. The call omits :report_errors, so PCRE's match_limit error is returned as :nomatch. The function compares the result to :match and returns false for a genuine non-match and for an exhausted budget alike.

2. Keyword evaluation. JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Validation.validate_keyword/3 uses the result for pattern, and JSV.Vocabulary.V202012.Applicator uses it to decide which patternProperties subschemas apply to each key. The draft 7 vocabulary delegates to the same modules. A false from an exhausted budget therefore means a pattern keyword fails and a patternProperties subschema is skipped.

3. Inversion by combinators. Under not, anyOf, oneOf, if and contains, a failing subschema can make the parent succeed, so a false non-match under not accepts a string the deny-list should reject. Under patternProperties the skipped subschema means the value is checked against additionalProperties or nothing.

4. History. Before the budget was introduced, the same keywords called Regex.match?/2, which also returns false on Erlang's default limit of 10,000,000 steps. The budget lowered the input size needed from about 25 bytes to about 20 bytes for the advisory's pattern.

cna.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies

solutions.value: Upgrade to HTTP-Body 1.24_01 or later.

descriptions.value:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies.

In chunked mode, used when no content length is given, add() holds each chunk in memory until all of it has arrived. A line that is not a chunk-size line, a size line without CRLF, or a size too large to fit an integer leaves the parser waiting forever, and every later add() grows the buffer.

A remote attacker can exhaust memory in applications that pass chunked request bodies to HTTP::Body.

descriptions.value:
Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in benoitc idna allows an attacker who controls a hostname passed to the library to exhaust CPU via an over-long xn-- label. idna:ulabel/1 in src/idna.erl hands every ASCII label that starts with xn-- to punycode:decode/1 without applying check_label_length/1, the 63-octet DNS label limit. punycode:decode/1 in src/punycode.erl builds its output with list appends in insert/4, so its cost grows super-linearly with the label length. A label of a few kilobytes keeps a scheduler busy for seconds to minutes before the label is rejected as invalid punycode.

Every decode entry point reaches this path: decode/1, decode/2, to_unicode/1 and from_ascii/1. The encode path reaches it as well, because alabel/1 calls ulabel/1 on an ASCII xn-- label before its own length check, so encode/1, encode/2 and to_ascii/1 are affected for such input.

This issue affects idna: from 0.5.0 before 8.0.0.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Label dispatch. idna:decode/2 in src/idna.erl lowercases the domain, splits it into labels and passes each one to ulabel/1. For an all-ASCII label that starts with xn--, ulabel/1 strips the prefix and calls punycode:decode/1 on the remainder. No length check runs before that call. check_label_length/1, which rejects labels longer than 63 octets, is only called from alabel/1, and there only after alabel/1 has itself called ulabel/1 on an ASCII label.

2. Super-linear decoding. punycode:decode/1 in src/punycode.erl decodes one code point per delta and places it into the output with insert/4. insert/4 walks to the insertion index by rebuilding the head with Head ++ [C] on every step and then appends the tail with another ++. Each insertion therefore costs time quadratic in the insertion index, and the total work grows roughly with the cube of the label length. The reporter measured about an 8x increase in running time per doubling of the label.

3. Work before rejection. The crafted label is not valid punycode and the call eventually exits with an error, but only after the decoder has processed the whole label. The ?MAX overflow guards in punycode:decode/1 cover the RFC 3492 integer overflow class and do not bound the running time.

4. Entry points. decode/1, decode/2, to_unicode/1 and from_ascii/1 reach ulabel/1 in every affected release. From 6.0.0, alabel/1 calls ulabel/1 on any ASCII label that starts with xn-- before check_label_length/1, so encode/1, encode/2, to_ascii/1 and utf8_to_ascii/1 reach the decoder for such input as well.

cna.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload

solutions.value: Upgrade to HTTP-Body 1.24_01 or later.

descriptions.value:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload.

For every file part, the multipart parser finds the suffix of the uploaded filename by matching the default $basename_regexp, qr/[^.]+(\.[^\\\/]+)$/, against the whole basename. A basename made of many dots and ending in a backslash makes the regex backtrack in time quadratic in its length.

A remote attacker can exhaust CPU with one request, as a basename of about 32 KB takes several seconds to match and every file part is matched separately.

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch vulnerability in deadtrickster ssl_verify_fun allows an adversary in the middle to impersonate a TLS peer via a certificate that carries a partial-label wildcard. try_match_wildcard/4 in src/ssl_verify_hostname.erl anchors only the text before and after the * of an identifier such as f*.example.net, so the wildcard also consumes dots and the certificate is accepted for f.evil.example.net. RFC 6125 confines a wildcard to the left-most label. The same matcher lets *.168.1.1 match the IP literal 192.168.1.1. Whole-label wildcards are matched correctly.

Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later check the hostname in ssl before a user verify_fun sees valid_peer, so a client that keeps server_name_indication set rejects the mismatch regardless. Exposed are clients that disable SNI, servers that verify client certificate hostnames with this library, and direct callers of verify_cert_hostname/2.

This issue affects ssl_verify_fun: from 1.0.1 before 1.1.8.

configurations.value: ssl_verify_fun decides the outcome only where it is the sole hostname check. Erlang/OTP 20.0 and later verify the hostname in ssl before the user verify_fun is called with valid_peer, as long as server_name_indication is a hostname or the connection was upgraded from a socket. A deployment is exposed when it sets {server_name_indication, disable}, when a TLS server uses ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3 to verify client certificates, when it calls ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname/2 directly, or when it runs Erlang/OTP older than 20.0. The attacker also needs a certificate with a partial-label wildcard from a CA the client trusts, which the CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements do not allow, so the realistic exposure is private PKI.

x_proofOfConcept.value:
* Issue a leaf certificate whose only subjectAltName entry is dNSName f*.example.net, for example with public_key:pkix_test_data/1, and decode it with public_key:pkix_decode_cert(Der, otp).
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "foo.example.net"). It returns {valid, "foo.example.net"}, as expected.
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "f.evil.example.net"). It returns {valid, "f.evil.example.net"} although the hostname spans two labels where the wildcard sits.
* Call ssl_verify_hostname:verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "a.b.example.net") as a control. It returns {fail, unable_to_match_altnames}.
* For the IP-literal variant, issue a leaf with dNSName *.168.1.1 and call verify_cert_hostname(Cert, "192.168.1.1"). It returns {valid, "192.168.1.1"}.
* To observe the full TLS path, serve the first certificate from ssl:listen/2 and connect with {verify, verify_peer}, the CA in cacerts, {verify_fun, {fun ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3, [{check_hostname, "f.evil.example.net"}]}} and {server_name_indication, disable}. The handshake succeeds. With {server_name_indication, "f.evil.example.net"} instead, OTP 20.0 or later rejects the certificate with hostname_check_failed before ssl_verify_fun runs.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Identifier parsing. ssl_verify_hostname:try_match_hostname/2 strips trailing dots, tries an exact case-insensitive match, and otherwise calls parse_and_validate_wildcard_identifier/2. That function accepts an identifier with one * in the left-most label and at least two labels after it, and classifies it as SingleCharW when the label is exactly *.

2. Whole-label wildcard, correct. For *.example.net the matcher compares the text after the * with the hostname from its first dot onward, so a.b.example.net fails because .b.example.net differs from .example.net.

3. Partial-label wildcard, incorrect. For f*.example.net the SingleCharW branch is skipped. try_match_wildcard/4 then checks only that the hostname ends with .example.net and starts with f. Nothing checks the span consumed by the *, so f.evil.example.net and f.a.b.example.net pass. RFC 6125 section 6.4.3 limits a wildcard to the left-most label. The wildcard_not_in_a_label/2 guard only rejects internationalized xn-- labels and does not help.

4. IP literals. The reference identifier is treated as a DNS name whatever its shape, so verify_cert_hostname/2 with hostname 192.168.1.1 matches a dNSName of *.168.1.1 through the whole-label branch. RFC 6125 does not apply wildcard matching to IP addresses, and OTP's ssl converts an IP-literal string to an {ip, ...} reference that only matches iPAddress entries.

5. Interaction with Erlang/OTP. When ssl_verify_hostname:verify_fun/3 is used as verify_fun, OTP 20.0 and later call ssl_certificate:validate/4 for valid_peer before the user fun. In the client role with server_name_indication set to a hostname, or with a peer IP from a socket upgrade, OTP runs public_key:pkix_verify_hostname/3 and hands the user fun {bad_cert, hostname_check_failed} instead of valid_peer, which ssl_verify_fun turns into {fail, ...}. OTP's default match function allows no wildcards, and its https match function (public_key:pkix_verify_hostname_match_fun/1) splits both names on dots and matches the wildcard within the first label only. The ssl_verify_fun result therefore decides the outcome only with {server_name_indication, disable}, in the server role, on direct calls to verify_cert_hostname/2, or on OTP older than 20.0.

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Ahmed Hesham Salah (SecuriCIP) for reporting this issue.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the Pushed Authorization Request PAR implementation of the keycloak-services component. The issue occurs when an authentication flow is restarted, which incorrectly clears the internal markers used to track PAR consumption while leaving the request active. This allows an attacker to reuse the same authorization request to obtain multiple access tokens, bypassing security requirements for single-use requests.

cna.title: @fastify/secure-session vulnerable to signature verification bypass via cookie signature removal

descriptions.value: @fastify/secure-session is a session plugin for Fastify that stores an encrypted session in a cookie. In versions 7.5.0 through 8.4.1, when the plugin is configured with the signed cookie option, it calls the cookie unsign routine but, when the signature check reports the value as invalid, still passes the original cookie value to the session decoder, so a session whose signature did not validate is decrypted anyway. The practical effect appears when an application supplies the cookie signing secret independently of the session encryption key and rotates only the signing secret to retire existing sessions while keeping the encryption key active, because a holder of an old session cookie can strip the now obsolete signature and keep using the session. The attacker must already possess an unexpired encrypted session cookie and needs neither secret, and cannot forge session data, extend expiry, or survive rotation of the encryption key. The issue is fixed in @fastify/secure-session 8.4.2, which no longer decodes the session when the signed cookie option is set and the signature check fails, and users should upgrade to 8.4.2 or later. As a workaround, rotate the session encryption key rather than relying on rotation of the cookie signing secret alone.

descriptions.value: Janus WebRTC Server 1.2.3 through 1.4.0 is vulnerable to Directory Traversal. The application accepts a caller supplied media path when an ondemand stream is created. The path is validated only by checking whether it contains one of the audio extensions and is then passed to the file source which opens it. No canonicalization is performed and no directory allowlist is enforced, so an unauthenticated caller can make the server open an arbitrary local file and use it as a media source, with the content delivered to viewers as RTP audio.

descriptions.value:
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_html allows an attacker who controls attribute names to inject attributes and script into rendered HTML via Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1.

attributes_escape/1 in lib/phoenix_html.ex escapes attribute values but not attribute names. key_escape/1 passes a binary key through html_escape, which neutralizes quotes and angle brackets but not whitespace, so a key such as x onmouseover ends the attribute and starts a new one. An atom key is only dasherized, so any character passes, including quotes and >. Nested data, aria and phx keys take the same paths. An application is affected when it builds attribute keys from untrusted input and renders them through HEEx <tag {@attrs}>, content_tag/3, or a direct call. Before 3.0.0 the same code lived in Phoenix.HTML.Tag.

This issue affects phoenix_html: from 1.0.0 before 3.3.5 and from 4.0.0 before 4.4.0.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Attribute rendering. Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1 walks the key-value pairs through build_attrs/1 and nested_attrs/3 and emits each as key_escape(k)="attr_escape(v)". Values are escaped. Names are not checked against the HTML attribute-name grammar.

2. Binary names. key_escape/1 sends a binary through Phoenix.HTML.Engine.html_escape/1, which replaces &, <, >, " and '. Whitespace passes. HTML uses whitespace to separate attributes, so %{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"} renders  x onmouseover="alert(1)": a harmless x attribute followed by an attacker-chosen event handler.

3. Atom names. key_escape/1 converts an atom with Atom.to_string/1 and replaces _ with -. Nothing is escaped, so [{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}] renders  x" onclick="alert(1)="y" and aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}] renders  aria-x"><script>="y", which leaves the tag entirely. This path needs the application to create atoms from untrusted input, for example Jason.decode!(body, keys: :atoms) or String.to_atom/1 on a parameter.

4. Reachability. HEEx compiles <div {@attrs}> to a call to Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1 through Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine and Phoenix.LiveView.TagEngine. tag/2 and content_tag/3 in Phoenix.HTML.Tag (phoenix_html 1.x to 3.x) and in PhoenixHTMLHelpers.Tag (4.x) render attributes the same way. Versions before 3.0.0 emitted the dasherized name without any escaping at all.

**1. Attribute rendering.** `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` walks the key-value pairs through `build_attrs/1` and `nested_attrs/3` and emits each as `key_escape(k)="attr_escape(v)"`. Values are escaped. Names are not checked against the HTML attribute-name grammar.

**2. Binary names.** `key_escape/1` sends a binary through `Phoenix.HTML.Engine.html_escape/1`, which replaces `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`. Whitespace passes. HTML uses whitespace to separate attributes, so `%{"x onmouseover" => "alert(1)"}` renders ` x onmouseover="alert(1)"`: a harmless `x` attribute followed by an attacker-chosen event handler.

**3. Atom names.** `key_escape/1` converts an atom with `Atom.to_string/1` and replaces `_` with `-`. Nothing is escaped, so `[{:"x\" onclick=\"alert(1)", "y"}]` renders ` x" onclick="alert(1)="y"` and `aria: [{:"x\"><script>", "y"}]` renders ` aria-x"><script>="y"`, which leaves the tag entirely. This path needs the application to create atoms from untrusted input, for example `Jason.decode!(body, keys: :atoms)` or `String.to_atom/1` on a parameter.

**4. Reachability.** HEEx compiles `<div {@attrs}>` to a call to `Phoenix.HTML.attributes_escape/1` through `Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine` and `Phoenix.LiveView.TagEngine`. `tag/2` and `content_tag/3` in `Phoenix.HTML.Tag` (phoenix_html 1.x to 3.x) and in `PhoenixHTMLHelpers.Tag` (4.x) render attributes the same way. Versions before 3.0.0 emitted the dasherized name without any escaping at all.

cna.title: @fastify/session vulnerable to session revocation bypass via a logout race condition

descriptions.value: @fastify/session is a session plugin for Fastify. In all releases before 11.1.6, with the default rolling session behavior, a request that restored a session before a logout could save its own copy after another request had completed the session destroy call, recreating the destroyed session identifier with its authenticated data. An attacker who already holds a victim's valid signed session cookie and keeps a request in flight across the logout can replay that cookie to restore the session after it was meant to be revoked, without any cookie theft or signature forgery. The issue is fixed in @fastify/session 11.1.6, which adds a per session generation marker and a conditional store write so a session restored before a logout or regeneration cannot recreate or overwrite the current entry, and users should upgrade to 11.1.6 or later. There is no workaround, and custom session stores must implement the new conditional write.

cna.title: Keycloak-services: keycloak-services: saml redirect binding signature bypass via percent-encoded parameter names

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Mayssen Aidoudi (Think-it GmbH) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to align query parameter parsing between signature verification and request processing in Keycloak's SAML HTTP-Redirect binding so percent-encoded parameter names cannot evade signature checks: upgrade to the fixed Rhbk/Keycloak Rhel/Keycloak Services builds, which eliminates the parsing discrepancy between raw query parameter signature verification and decoded parameter processing in the SAML redirect binding, closing crafted HTTP GET request containing a percent-encoded unsigned SAML parameter placed before a legitimately signed parameter. Until patched, this is a concern on Keycloak instances configured to use SAML HTTP-Redirect binding for federated identity, so Audit and restrict account registration on external Identity Providers to prevent attackers from capturing legitimately signed redirect-binding messages. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying SAML parameter parsing discrepancy signature bypass — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding implementation of Keycloak. The issue occurs because the server processes percent-encoded parameter names (like %53AMLResponse) while the signature verification logic only checks literal parameter names. An attacker can use this discrepancy to provide a crafted, unsigned SAML message that the server processes instead of a legitimately signed one, leading to full account takeover of federated users.

references.name: Fix backport to release/v28: go-gitea/gitea pull request #39853

descriptions.value: The OCI registry's cross-repository blob mount checked the target package against the token's `public-only` restriction, but checked the source blob only against the full account permissions of the token owner. A `public-only` token with `write:package` scope, whose owner can read a private package and write to a public package namespace, could mount a blob of the private package into the public package. The private blob, such as a container layer, could then be downloaded by anyone through the public package.

cna.title: 389-ds-base: 389-ds-base: null pointer dereference via modifydn using an attribute's schema alias name causes denial of service

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Chad Sikorra for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Administrators should review custom access control instructions (ACIs) and avoid granting the ModifyDN (rename) right to non-administrative principals unless specifically required. Restricting this right reduces exposure to this issue until a fixed package is available. Neither 389-ds-base's own default ACI templates nor Red Hat Identity Management (IdM/FreeIPA)'s default ACIs grant this right to non-administrative users, so deployments that have not customized their ACIs are not exposed.

descriptions.value: A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in 389-ds-base. This flaw occurs when a ModifyDN (rename) operation uses an attribute's schema alias name (such as "commonName") instead of its canonical name (such as "cn") as the new relative distinguished name. An authenticated attacker with the ModifyDN (rename) permission on the affected entry can use this flaw to crash the directory server, causing a denial of service.

descriptions.value: An attacker with any Apple ID can sign in to an application that uses the Apple strategy as any other user whose Apple subject or email they know. Account lookup, account linking, and email-based access control then act on the attacker-chosen identity.

references.name: Unverified Sign in with Apple callback parameter can override verified ID token claims

workarounds.value: Remove the user parameter from the callback parameters before you pass them to Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2, for example with Map.delete(params, "user"). descriptions.value:
Acceptance of Extraneous Untrusted Data With Trusted Data vulnerability in the Sign in with Apple strategy in pow-auth Assent allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to impersonate another user via the user parameter of the authorization callback.

Apple posts the user's name to the callback endpoint in a user form parameter that the browser submits and the client controls. Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2 in lib/assent/strategies/apple.ex decodes that parameter, and fetch_user/2 merges it over the claims of the verified ID token, so the unverified map wins. An attacker who completes a Sign in with Apple login with their own Apple ID and edits the user parameter can replace sub, email, and any other claim. Applications that look up, link, or authorize accounts by the returned subject or email then act on the attacker's values.

This issue affects assent: from 0.1.25 before 0.3.2.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Unverified input. Apple's form_post response mode delivers code, id_token, state, and on the first authorization a user parameter that holds a JSON object with the user's name and email. The browser submits this parameter and Apple does not sign it, so the client controls its content.

2. Merge over verified claims. Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2 decodes the user parameter with Helpers.decode_json/2 and stores the map in the config under :user. After Assent.Strategy.OIDC.fetch_user/2 has validated the ID token, Assent.Strategy.Apple.fetch_user/2 calls Map.merge/2 with the verified claims first and the decoded parameter second. Keys from the parameter overwrite keys from the token, including sub and email.

3. Result. normalize/2 reads sub and email from the merged map and sets email_verified to true, so the application receives attacker-chosen identity fields marked as verified.

4. Fix. Version 0.3.2 ignores the parameter by default. With include_unverified_name: true, only given_name and family_name are taken from it, and the verified claims are merged over them.

Unverified input.** Apple's `form_post` response mode delivers `code`, `id_token`, `state`, and on the first authorization a `user` parameter that holds a JSON object with the user's name and email. The browser submits this parameter and Apple does not sign it, so the client controls its content.

**2. Merge over verified claims.** `Assent.Strategy.Apple.callback/2` decodes the `user` parameter with `Helpers.decode_json/2` and stores the map in the config under `:user`. After `Assent.Strategy.OIDC.fetch_user/2` has validated the ID token, `Assent.Strategy.Apple.fetch_user/2` calls `Map.merge/2` with the verified claims first and the decoded parameter second. Keys from the parameter overwrite keys from the token, including `sub` and `email`.

**3. Result.** `normalize/2` reads `sub` and `email` from the merged map and sets `email_verified` to true, so the application receives attacker-chosen identity fields marked as verified.

**4. Fix.** Version 0.3.2 ignores the parameter by default. With `include_unverified_name: true`, only `given_name` and `family_name` are taken from it, and the verified claims are merged over them.

cna.title: @fastify/multipart vulnerable to Denial of Service via a malformed upload hanging delayed file consumers

descriptions.value: @fastify/multipart is the multipart form-data and file upload plugin for the Fastify web framework. In versions 5.3.0 through 10.1.6, the plugin does not propagate a parser error to the file stream when a request body ends inside a file part with no closing boundary, even though the Content-Length is complete, the client does not abort, and no file size limit is exceeded. The plugin destroys the in-progress file stream without an error, so a handler that iterates the request parts and performs asynchronous work before consuming the file attaches to a stream that never emits an error or end event, and the request never responds while the connection stays open. An unauthenticated remote client can repeat these malformed uploads against such a route to accumulate pending connections and exhaust server resources, so the impact is availability only and exploitation depends on the application using a delayed file consumer. The issue is fixed in @fastify/multipart 10.1.7, where the parser error is propagated to the file stream so a delayed consumer settles with an error instead of hanging, and users should upgrade to 10.1.7 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading.

cna.title: URL prefix handling permits API key read-scope bypass in Psono Server

descriptions.value: A write-only API key could read encrypted secret records through the bulk-secret-read endpoint despite having its read scope disabled.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to Psono Server 7.2.4 or later.

descriptions.value: Psono Server CE && EE versions 4.0.33 through 7.2.3 compared the request path for the bulk-secret-read endpoint with a hard-coded unprefixed path. In deployments configured with URL_PREFIX, the comparison failed and the POST request was authorized using write scope instead of read scope. An authenticated remote attacker with an unusual read-disabled, write-enabled API key could therefore retrieve encrypted secret data and nonces through the prefixed bulk-secret-read endpoint despite lacking read permission. The default configuration without URL_PREFIX was not affected.

descriptions.value: The File Manager plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file deletion due to insufficient file path validation in the connector function in all versions from 6.0 - 6.9. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to read and delete arbitrary files on the server, which can lead to remote code execution when the right file is deleted (such as wp-config.php). The bypass is triggered by passing cmd=rm or cmf=file in the URL query string of a POST request: elFinder's bind registration reads the command exclusively from $_POST and therefore never registers the rm.pre permission handler, while the dispatcher reads from the merged $_GET+$_POST superglobal and executes the rm or file command unchecked against a volume that defaults to ABSPATH.

workarounds.value: Until upgrading, only run `nvm ls-remote` and LTS-refreshing commands against trusted mirrors over TLS, and ensure `NVM_NODEJS_ORG_MIRROR` and `NVM_IOJS_ORG_MIRROR` point only at trusted endpoints.

descriptions.value: Node Version Manager (nvm) is a POSIX-compliant shell function for managing multiple node.js versions. In versions 0.32.1 through 0.40.5, `nvm ls-remote` (and other commands that refresh remote LTS aliases, such as `nvm install --lts`) parse the node.js mirror's `index.tab` and use each release's LTS codename field as an alias filename without validating it. A malicious, compromised, or man-in-the-middled mirror can return an LTS codename containing path-traversal sequences such as `../../../.bashrc`, causing nvm to write the associated version string to a path outside `$NVM_DIR/alias`. With the default layout (`$NVM_DIR` is `~/.nvm`), this can create or overwrite files in the user's home directory, including shell startup files, which can lead to code execution in a later shell session. Exploitation requires the victim to use a hostile mirror -- via a compromised mirror or CDN, a network man-in-the-middle, or a maliciously configured `NVM_NODEJS_ORG_MIRROR`/`NVM_IOJS_ORG_MIRROR` -- and to run an affected command. Version 0.40.6 validates remote LTS codenames as safe alias filenames and rejects `..` path components when writing alias files.

cna.title: Type confusion in Zephyr HL78xx GNSS NMEA driver causes wild-pointer write from GNSS input

descriptions.value:
The Sierra Wireless HL78xx modem GNSS driver (drivers/modem/hl78xx/, later drivers/modem/vendor_standalone/hl78xx/) embeds a generic struct gnss_nmea0183_match_data match_data inside struct hl78xx_gnss_data. The generic NMEA0183 match helper (drivers/gnss/gnss_nmea0183_match.c) requires that context to be the first member because its callbacks cast user_data directly to struct gnss_nmea0183_match_data . In the affected releases match_data was the second member (after const struct device dev), so it sat at a non-zero offset while gnss_nmea0183_match_init() initialized it at the correct address. The registered NMEA handlers instead pass the whole device data object (data->devices.gnss->data, offset 0), producing an offset-shifted type confusion between where state is initialized and where the parse callbacks read and write it.

When NMEA sentences from the GNSS receiver are parsed, the GGA/RMC callbacks write parsed fix data into the wrong location within the struct, and the GSV callback (gnss_nmea0183_match_gsv_callback, active under CONFIG_GNSS_SATELLITES) reads its satellites pointer and bound from the wrong offsets — non-pointer bytes of struct hl78xx_gnss_data — and then writes parsed struct gnss_satellite entries through that bogus pointer. This is a write through an uninitialized/wild pointer with a garbage bound.

The NMEA handlers are registered by default (CONFIG_HL78XX_GNSS_SOURCE_NMEA is the default GNSS source) on devices using the HL78xx GNSS. The driver runs in kernel context and the NMEA data originates from the GNSS radio front-end, so a party able to influence the GNSS signal (for example GNSS/GPS spoofing at radio proximity) can drive the kernel-side parser into the faulty write. The most likely impact is a crash (denial of service) because the bogus pointer resolves to a fixed near-NULL value, with adjacent-memory corruption possible on MMU-less targets. Confidentiality is not affected. Exploitation requires the satellites feature to be enabled and active, so attack complexity is high.

cna.title: Kronosnet: kronosnet: encryption key exposure in memory after cryptographic configuration changes

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Fabio Di Nitto for reporting this issue.

descriptions.value: A vulnerability was found in kronosnet's (version <=1.34) cryptographic configuration management. The framework does not correctly zero-out or wipe sensitive memory segments after executing changes to its cryptographic configuration. This omission leaves raw encryption keys resident in memory after the associated structures are freed. A local attacker capable of leveraging memory disclosure techniques could exploit this flaw to retrieve the active encryption key, allowing them to decrypt cluster network communications or inject malicious packets to cause severe high-availability cluster instability.

cna.title: Server-side file-write and request forgery via spatial lookups

descriptions.value: CAPEC-664: Server Side Request Forgery

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.17 and 6.0 before 6.0.8.
GeoDjango spatial lookups optimistically parse the right-hand-side value as a raster by passing it to the `django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster` constructor. Any value used in a spatial lookup against a `GeometryField` or `RasterField` reaches this constructor, including untrusted input, for example a spatial-field filter submitted through the Django admin changelist query string by a staff user with view permission. A `dict`, or a `str` holding its JSON representation, is opened in write mode regardless of the constructor's `write=False` default, allowing a file with an attacker-chosen name and contents to be written through a file-backed GDAL driver. Any other `str` is treated as a datasource, allowing an outbound network request through a GDAL virtual filesystem handler. Writing a file to a location later imported by the application can result in remote code execution.
Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.1.x, 5.0.x, and 4.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.
Django would like to thank Bence Nagy, localhost-detect, and kimchunbok_ for reporting this issue.

cna.title: User Profile Builder <= 3.16.4 - Unauthenticated Authentication Bypass via Type Confusion to Administrator Account Takeover via 'username' Parameter

affected.product: User Profile Builder – Beautiful User Registration Forms, User Profiles & User Role Editor

descriptions.value: The User Profile Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via Type Confusion in versions up to, and including, 3.16.4. This is due to the wppb_log_in_user() function calling absint() on the return value of wp_insert_user() before performing an is_wp_error() check — when a registration is submitted with a 61–70 character username, WordPress core rejects it with a WP_Error object, but absint() coerces that object to the integer 1 before the error check can short-circuit execution, causing the plugin to bind and return a transient-backed autologin nonce tied to user ID 1. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as the site's Administrator account (user ID 1), resulting in full administrative takeover of the site.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Netskope Client and Endpoint DLP version R142.0.0 or later, or apply the appropriate maintenance update: R141 (141.1.13.2833 and above), R138 (138.1.16.2834 and above), or R135 (135.1.27.2835 and above).

workarounds.value: Restrict folder and file creation permissions for unprivileged users on the root of secondary volumes using Windows Access Control Lists (icacls). Endpoints without secondary drives are not susceptible.

supportingMedia.value: Restrict folder and file creation permissions for unprivileged users on the root of secondary volumes using Windows Access Control Lists (icacls). Endpoints without secondary drives are not susceptible.

descriptions.value: An uncontrolled search path vulnerability (CWE-427) in statically linked OpenSSL libraries within Netskope Client (stAgentSvc.exe) and Endpoint DLP (epdlp.exe) on Windows allows an authenticated local attacker to execute arbitrary code with elevated SYSTEM privileges. The services retain internal build-time paths referencing a secondary drive location. On Windows systems where default volume permissions allow standard users to create root-level directories on secondary drives, an attacker can place a malicious configuration file (openssl.cnf) that is loaded under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM context upon service startup or system reboot. Under default operating system permissions, macOS and Linux are not susceptible, and mobile platforms are unaffected.

cna.title: SMS Alert <= 3.9.7 - Authenticated (Administrator+) SQL Injection via 'checkout_payment_plans' and 'order_status' Settings

affected.product: SMS Alert – SMS & OTP for WooCommerce, Order Notifications & Abandoned Cart Recovery

descriptions.value: The SMS Alert – SMS & OTP for WooCommerce, Order Notifications & Abandoned Cart Recovery plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to generic SQL Injection via 'checkout_payment_plans' and 'order_status' Settings in all versions up to, and including, 3.9.7 due to insufficient escaping on the user supplied parameter and lack of sufficient preparation on the existing SQL query. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with administrator-level access and above, to append additional SQL queries into already existing queries that can be used to extract sensitive information from the database. This is a second-order SQL injection: the malicious payload is stored in the 'checkout_payment_plans' and 'order_status' settings via update_option() and executed later when the cod_to_prepaid_cart_notification_sendsms_hook WP-Cron event fires SA_CodTOPrepaid::sendSms().

descriptions.value: CAPEC-201

In Eclipse RDF4J, several XML parser entry points do not fully restrict XML External Entity (XXE) processing when parsing untrusted XML-based RDF data or query results, permitting DOCTYPE declarations, external entity references, and external DTD loading. This is due to an incomplete fix for CVE-2018-1000644: the earlier fix did not cover all parser entry points. The issue is resolved in RDF4J 5.3.2, which rejects or disables DOCTYPE declarations, external entities, and external DTD loading by default.
